one_line: Backbone-scaling gains in semantic segmentation are largely effective-resolution artifacts, not representation gains.
problem: Papers report that larger ViT backbones segment better, but larger models are routinely evaluated with more tokens per image (finer patch grids, higher input resolution), confounding scale with effective resolution.
core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of the reported model-size gain on dense benchmarks comes from the token-grid difference, not from richer representations; at matched token counts the scaling curve flattens sharply.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating one public ViT family (S/B/L) on ADE20K with token grids matched across sizes will remove at least half of the B-to-L mIoU gap reported under default settings.
why_important: If true, practitioners buying larger backbones for dense tasks are mostly buying resolution they could get far cheaper, and scaling studies for dense prediction need a resolution-controlled protocol.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: resolution confounds are discussed informally, but I am not aware of a systematic token-matched re-measurement of backbone scaling curves specifically for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take publicly released checkpoints of one backbone family, fine-tune identical decoders on ADE20K at two token-grid settings (default vs matched), and compare the size-vs-mIoU slopes.
main_risk: Matching token grids may force some models off their pretraining resolution, introducing a new confound (resolution shift penalty) that has to be controlled with brief re-adaptation.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Bigger backbones intrinsically produce better dense predictions; scaling curves reported for segmentation reflect representation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap may persist at matched token counts because large models genuinely encode better local features, in which case the confound is real but small.
fastest_falsification: One GPU-week: two token settings, three model sizes, one dataset, identical decoder and schedule; compare slopes.

one_line: Pretraining-data scaling saturates for dense transfer long before it saturates for classification transfer.
problem: The community extrapolates classification-style data-scaling benefits to dense tasks, but dense transfer may stop improving orders of magnitude earlier in pretraining-set size.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation fine-tuning consumes mostly mid-level features that saturate with modest pretraining data; beyond that, extra pretraining images improve linear-probe classification but not downstream mIoU.
falsifiable_prediction: For checkpoints pretrained on nested data subsets, downstream segmentation mIoU will plateau (delta under 0.3 mIoU per data doubling) at least two doublings before linear-probe classification accuracy plateaus.
why_important: Data-scaling budgets for dense-task foundation models may be wildly misallocated; a verified early plateau redirects spend toward resolution, annotation quality, or decoder design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: scaling-law papers exist for classification and some for detection; a decoupling analysis contrasting dense-vs-classification saturation points on identical checkpoints appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use one SSL recipe on nested subsets (1%, 10%, 100% of a public corpus), fine-tune the same segmentation head on two benchmarks, and plot both transfer curves against pretraining size.
main_risk: Saturation point may depend strongly on the SSL objective chosen, limiting generality of a single-recipe result.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: More pretraining data monotonically and materially improves all downstream tasks including segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense transfer may track classification transfer closely because both ride the same feature quality; the plateau may be an artifact of small fine-tuning sets rather than pretraining.
fastest_falsification: Reuse publicly released checkpoints trained on different data fractions where available; fine-tune segmentation heads only, a few GPU-days.

one_line: Boundary quality anti-scales: bigger segmentation models get relatively worse at boundaries as they get better at regions.
problem: Progress is tracked with region metrics (mIoU); if scale buys context at the expense of localization, the field is optimizing away from boundary fidelity without noticing.
core_hypothesis: Larger models rely more on global context and low-frequency evidence, so their boundary-F to mIoU ratio decreases with scale within a model family.
falsifiable_prediction: Across at least two public model families spanning 3+ sizes, boundary-F1 normalized by mIoU will decrease monotonically with model size on Cityscapes and ADE20K.
why_important: Boundary fidelity is what downstream users (editing, robotics grasping, medical margins) actually consume; an anti-scaling law here would redirect scaling investments.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: boundary metrics are reported sporadically; a systematic scale-vs-boundary-ratio law across families does not appear to have been established or refuted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-score publicly released checkpoints of two segmentation families at three sizes each with boundary-F and mIoU; test monotonicity of the ratio.
main_risk: Boundary-F differences may sit within ground-truth boundary annotation noise on these benchmarks, requiring a high-precision relabeled subset to resolve.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Scaling improves segmentation quality across the board, including boundary quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger models often also carry higher-resolution features, which could improve boundaries in absolute and relative terms, breaking the predicted monotonicity.
fastest_falsification: Pure re-scoring of existing checkpoints; no training. One day of compute plus metric code.

one_line: Web-scale pretraining makes long-tail segmentation classes worse, not better, past a data threshold.
problem: Scaling web data is assumed to help rare categories via coverage, but web frequency distributions may increasingly drown tail-class features under head-class statistics.
core_hypothesis: Past a corpus size, marginal web images are overwhelmingly head-class content; continued pretraining shifts feature allocation toward head classes and measurably degrades frozen-feature separability for tail segmentation classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Frozen-feature probes for the rarest quartile of LVIS-style mask categories will peak at an intermediate pretraining-data scale and decline at the largest scale, while head-class probes rise monotonically.
why_important: If tail performance anti-scales, the standard remedy (pretrain on more web data) is actively harmful for the classes that matter in specialized deployments.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: head-class dominance is documented for classification training sets; an anti-scaling effect on tail-class dense transfer across pretraining scales appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe frozen features from checkpoints of one family pretrained on increasing data scales with linear masks decoders on a long-tail instance benchmark, stratify by class frequency.
main_risk: Publicly available checkpoint series may confound data scale with training compute and recipe changes, requiring careful checkpoint selection or partial retraining.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: More pretraining data improves coverage of rare concepts and therefore helps long-tail downstream performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even rare concepts gain absolute example counts as the corpus grows, which may outweigh the relative dilution; tail probes may rise monotonically.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-probe evaluation only, no pretraining: a few GPU-days if suitable checkpoint series exist publicly.

one_line: Claimed emergent zero-shot segmentation abilities are thresholded-metric artifacts, not capability jumps.
problem: Emergence narratives (ability appears suddenly at scale) are migrating from language to vision; if the jump is an artifact of discontinuous metrics, scaling policy conclusions drawn from it are wrong.
core_hypothesis: Under continuous credit metrics (soft-IoU, per-pixel likelihood), zero-shot segmentation ability improves smoothly with scale; apparent emergence is created by success-threshold metrics such as IoU-above-0.5 counts.
falsifiable_prediction: For any model family showing a sharp scale jump under thresholded segmentation success rates, re-scoring the same outputs with soft-IoU will show a smooth curve with no statistically detectable breakpoint.
why_important: Emergence claims drive scale-first funding decisions; showing the vision version is a metric artifact would recalibrate expectations for dense-task scaling.
why_possibly_novel: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK exists arguing emergence-as-metric-artifact for language models; the segmentation-specific test on dense outputs is the unverified new part (HYPOTHESIS).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect zero-shot mask outputs from a scale series, score with both thresholded success rate and soft-IoU, fit breakpoint models to both curves and compare evidence for discontinuity.
main_risk: Few public scale series expose comparable zero-shot segmentation interfaces, limiting the families on which the claim can be tested.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Segmentation-relevant abilities emerge discontinuously at scale, justifying scale-first research strategies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some dense abilities could be genuinely discontinuous (for example, prompt-following behavior), and soft metrics might also show breakpoints, refuting the artifact account.
fastest_falsification: Re-scoring existing outputs with two metric families and a breakpoint test; days, no training.

one_line: Per-domain small specialists beat one large generalist segmenter at equal total inference cost.
problem: The field is consolidating on large generalist segmentation models, but deployments are usually domain-known at inference time, where the generalist premium may be negative.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed total parameter or FLOP budget spread over K known domains, K fine-tuned small models each beat the single K-times-larger generalist on their own domain, because generalists pay a capacity tax for cross-domain interference.
falsifiable_prediction: On a 5-domain suite (driving, indoor, aerial, medical, web images), five small specialists at budget B/5 each will beat one generalist at budget B on at least 4 of 5 domains.
why_important: Directly contradicts the consolidation trend and gives deployment engineers a defensible cheap alternative; also quantifies the real price of generality.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: specialist-vs-generalist comparisons exist informally, but a compute-matched, budget-fair version for segmentation across heterogeneous domains seems missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train one generalist and per-domain specialists from the same pretrained initialization under matched total budget; evaluate per-domain and report the win matrix.
main_risk: Result depends on the domain split granularity; adversarially fine splits favor specialists trivially, so domain definitions must be pre-registered.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: A single large model trained on everything is the strongest and most economical way to serve many segmentation domains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-domain transfer inside the generalist may outweigh interference, especially for low-data domains, making the generalist win exactly where it matters.
fastest_falsification: One pretrained backbone, five cheap fine-tunes plus one joint fine-tune at matched budget; about a GPU-week.

one_line: Scaling same-protocol annotation converges to protocol bias, not to ground truth.
problem: Datasets grow by adding more labels under one annotation protocol; if errors are protocol-systematic rather than random, more labels stop buying accuracy against reality.
core_hypothesis: Beyond a modest dataset size, models trained on more same-protocol masks improve on the protocol test set but not on an independent-protocol reference set, because remaining error is shared bias, not variance.
falsifiable_prediction: Training curves on 10x more same-protocol data will show continued gains on the native test set but statistically flat performance against a differently-protocoled re-annotation of the same test images.
why_important: Redefines what data scaling can achieve: past the bias floor, money should go to protocol diversity or re-annotation, not volume; this is a constructive anti-scaling law for labels.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: label noise is well studied as random noise; protocol-systematic bias as the asymptote of dataset scaling appears unquantified for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate 300 test images under a second written protocol with different boundary conventions; train models on nested fractions of the original set; compare gain curves against both references.
main_risk: Designing a second protocol that is genuinely independent rather than just noisier is hard; a sloppy protocol would fake the plateau.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: More annotated data keeps improving real-world segmentation quality; the test set measures that quality adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If annotation errors are mostly idiosyncratic per annotator, scaling continues to help against any reference, and the plateau never appears.
fastest_falsification: 300-image dual-protocol re-annotation plus existing checkpoints trained on data fractions; annotation cost dominates, compute is trivial.

one_line: Over-pretraining exists: dense transfer peaks and then degrades as SSL pretraining runs longer.
problem: Pretraining length is treated as monotonically beneficial (or at worst neutral) for downstream tasks; dense tasks may actually be harmed by late-stage pretraining dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Late SSL training increasingly collapses features toward the pretext task invariances (aggressive crop/color invariance), destroying localization-relevant information, so segmentation transfer is non-monotonic in pretraining epochs while classification probes keep rising.
falsifiable_prediction: Fine-tuned segmentation mIoU from intermediate checkpoints of a long SSL run will peak before the final checkpoint by a margin exceeding seed noise, while the linear classification probe of the same checkpoints is monotone.
why_important: Checkpoint selection for dense transfer would need its own early-stopping criterion, and compute spent on longer pretraining may be actively destructive for dense users.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: non-monotonic transfer has been hinted at in isolated ablations; establishing a robust dense-vs-classification divergence across recipes appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Save 8 checkpoints across one public SSL training trajectory, fine-tune an identical segmentation head from each, plot both transfer curves with 3 seeds.
main_risk: The effect may be recipe-specific (strong color augmentation recipes only), reducing it from a law to a footnote unless multiple recipes are tested.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Longer pretraining never hurts downstream fine-tuning; final checkpoints are the best checkpoints.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may fully recover any localization information lost during late pretraining, flattening the curve and refuting practical relevance.
fastest_falsification: If a public run releases intermediate checkpoints, this is a week of fine-tuning; otherwise one medium SSL run instrumented with checkpoint dumps.

one_line: Compute-optimal scaling recipes imported from language mispredict segmentation because resolution is the missing third axis.
problem: Teams allocate dense-model training compute using parameter-vs-data rules derived from language and classification, ignoring input resolution as a first-class scaling variable.
core_hypothesis: For segmentation pretraining and fine-tuning, reallocating FLOPs from parameters to input resolution beats the language-derived allocation across a wide budget range; the compute-optimal frontier is resolution-dominated.
falsifiable_prediction: At three fixed FLOP budgets, the best (params, data, resolution) triple found by grid search will spend at least 2x more relative compute on resolution than a Chinchilla-style params-data rule extended naively, and beat it by over 1 mIoU.
why_important: Provides a corrected, dense-specific compute-allocation rule; anti-scaling in the specific sense that parameter scaling is overrated for dense prediction.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: resolution scaling is studied piecemeal; a three-axis compute-optimal frontier for segmentation seems not to have been mapped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Small-scale 3-axis grid (3 param sizes x 3 data sizes x 3 resolutions) at matched FLOPs on one benchmark, fit the frontier, compare against the two-axis rule extrapolation.
main_risk: Grid is expensive even at small scale, and frontier shape may not extrapolate to production budgets without additional anchor runs.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Parameter and data scaling rules from language/classification transfer to dense tasks with minor adjustments.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Resolution gains may saturate quickly once ground-truth mask precision becomes the bottleneck, making the two-axis rule approximately correct after all.
fastest_falsification: A 27-cell mini-grid at deliberately small budget (each cell hours, not days) reveals whether resolution dominates the local frontier.

one_line: Diverse small-model ensembles beat scale-matched single large segmenters out of distribution, reversing the in-distribution verdict.
problem: Single large models have displaced ensembles based on in-distribution benchmarks; deployment failure is dominated by distribution shift where the comparison may flip.
core_hypothesis: Ensemble diversity provides error decorrelation that scale does not buy; under real shift (weather, geography, sensor), an ensemble of 3-4 heterogeneous small segmenters at matched total FLOPs beats the single large model that wins in-distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: On at least 3 of 4 shifted test sets (for example Cityscapes-trained models evaluated on other driving datasets, night, adverse weather), the matched-FLOP heterogeneous ensemble will beat the single large model, despite losing in-distribution.
why_important: Challenges the scale-consolidation narrative exactly where reliability matters, and revives a cheap classical tool with a precise regime claim.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: ensembles-vs-scale comparisons exist for classification accuracy and uncertainty; a FLOP-matched OOD segmentation showdown with heterogeneous members appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 3 small public segmenters with different backbones, average logits, match total FLOPs to one large public model, evaluate both on standard shifted driving benchmarks.
main_risk: Heterogeneous ensembles need output-space alignment (label taxonomies, resolutions); sloppy alignment could mask or fake the effect.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: A single large model dominates ensembles of small ones at matched compute, in and out of distribution.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large models may already act as implicit ensembles and shift-robustness may scale with size faster than diversity can compensate.
fastest_falsification: Public checkpoints only, no training: one day to run the four-way OOD comparison.

one_line: Boundary-aware loss functions stop beating plain cross-entropy once the baseline gets the same tuning budget.
problem: A large family of boundary-weighted and boundary-specific losses reports consistent gains, but baselines in those papers may be under-tuned relative to the proposed method.
core_hypothesis: Reported gains of the boundary-loss family are mostly asymmetric-tuning artifacts; with an equal hyperparameter search budget for plain cross-entropy plus standard tricks, the median gain across the family falls below the benchmark noise floor.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running 5+ representative boundary-loss variants and a cross-entropy baseline under an identical 30-trial search protocol on two benchmarks will yield a median boundary-loss gain under 0.3 mIoU and under 0.5 boundary-F.
why_important: If a whole loss family is a tuning mirage, reviewers and practitioners need matched-budget evaluation as a norm; if gains survive, the family earns a solid replication certificate.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: matched-budget re-evaluations exist in other subfields (metric learning, GANs); a rigorous one for segmentation boundary losses appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed backbone/decoder; grid or random search of equal size for each loss; 3 seeds; report gain distributions rather than best-vs-default comparisons.
main_risk: Choice of which variants represent the family is contestable; needs pre-registered selection criteria to avoid cherry-picking accusations in either direction.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Boundary-aware losses reliably improve segmentation, especially boundary quality, over cross-entropy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary losses may genuinely help on boundary metrics even under fair tuning, with only the mIoU gains evaporating; the family could be half-right.
fastest_falsification: Two losses (one classic, one recent) vs tuned CE with 30 trials each on one benchmark: about a GPU-week for a strong preliminary answer.

one_line: Mask-classification decoder heads owe most of their reported edge over per-pixel heads to training recipes, not architecture.
problem: The field has largely migrated from per-pixel decoders to query-based mask-classification decoders based on comparisons that changed recipes and heads simultaneously.
core_hypothesis: When a per-pixel head is trained with the exact modern recipe used by query-based heads (augmentation, longer schedules, losses, strong pretrained backbones), the architectural gap shrinks to a small residual on standard semantic benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Recipe-matched per-pixel heads will come within 1 mIoU of query-based heads on ADE20K semantic segmentation with identical backbones, versus the several-point gaps in original comparisons.
why_important: Correct attribution matters: if the recipe is the ingredient, simpler cheaper heads are viable, and future architecture claims need recipe-isolated ablations.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: partial recipe ablations exist in some papers; a clean full-recipe-transplant study across head types seems unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one query-based method's full training configuration, swap only the head for a per-pixel decoder of matched capacity, train both with 3 seeds on ADE20K and Cityscapes.
main_risk: Some recipe elements (Hungarian matching losses) do not transplant to per-pixel heads, forcing judgment calls about the fair analog.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Query-based mask-classification architectures are intrinsically superior to per-pixel prediction for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The residual gap may remain large on instance-aware tasks (panoptic), where set prediction is structurally advantaged, limiting the claim to semantic segmentation.
fastest_falsification: One recipe transplant on one dataset with 2 seeds: a few GPU-days for the headline number.

one_line: Test-time augmentation for segmentation loses to a single higher-resolution pass at matched inference FLOPs.
problem: Multi-scale plus flip TTA is a standard leaderboard ingredient, treated as free accuracy; its comparisons are never FLOP-matched against simpler ways to spend the same inference compute.
core_hypothesis: TTA gains are primarily a compute effect; spending the identical FLOPs on one larger-resolution (or sliding-window overlap) pass matches or beats TTA on modern models.
falsifiable_prediction: For 3 public models on 2 benchmarks, single-pass inference at TTA-FLOP-matched resolution will be within 0.2 mIoU of, or better than, standard multi-scale flip TTA in at least 5 of 6 conditions.
why_important: Deployment teams routinely skip TTA for latency; if TTA is just misallocated compute, papers should stop reporting it as a method contribution and leaderboards should FLOP-normalize.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: TTA is occasionally criticized informally; a FLOP-matched equivalence study on segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute TTA total FLOPs per image, find the single-pass resolution with equal FLOPs, evaluate both settings for several checkpoints, no training required.
main_risk: Models evaluated far above training resolution may degrade for resolution-shift reasons, unfairly penalizing the single-pass arm unless windowed inference is used.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: TTA extracts ensemble-like information that a single pass cannot, and its gains justify its cost for offline evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flip TTA specifically may add symmetry information unavailable at any single-pass resolution, preserving a real (if small) TTA edge.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only study: one afternoon per model-dataset pair.

one_line: Deep supervision and auxiliary segmentation heads are an optimizer-era relic with near-zero modern effect.
problem: Auxiliary losses on intermediate layers are still copied into new segmentation architectures as presumed-good practice inherited from earlier CNN training.
core_hypothesis: Auxiliary heads mattered when optimization of deep unnormalized networks was fragile; with modern normalization, initialization, and schedules, their gain is statistically indistinguishable from zero and occasionally negative.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating auxiliary heads across 4 modern architectures with 5 seeds each will produce mean absolute effects under 0.2 mIoU, within the cross-seed standard deviation, on both ADE20K and Cityscapes.
why_important: Every pointless component copied forward costs research clarity and compute; a clean negative result would prune a zombie practice and sharpen attribution in ablation tables.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: individual papers ablate their own auxiliary heads inconsistently; a dedicated multi-architecture replication with seed-level statistics appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 4 architectures with and without auxiliary losses, 5 seeds each, fixed recipes; report effect sizes with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Some architectures may secretly depend on auxiliary heads for stability at large learning rates, making the effect recipe-conditional rather than null.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Auxiliary deep-supervision heads provide small but real gains and should be included by default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Under long-schedule large-batch regimes the heads may still shape early optimization measurably; the null could fail exactly on the biggest models.
fastest_falsification: Two architectures, 3 seeds, one dataset: a weekend of compute for a strong preliminary verdict.

one_line: CRF and refinement post-processing now hurts as often as it helps, with a predictable flip point in backbone quality.
problem: Refinement modules validated on weak backbones are still bolted onto modern pipelines without re-validation, on the belief that sharpening boundaries is always safe.
core_hypothesis: Refinement injects a low-level appearance prior that corrected weak models but overrides correct semantic evidence in strong ones; there exists a backbone-quality threshold above which expected refinement gain is negative.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a ladder of 6 checkpoints of increasing quality, per-image refinement gain distributions will shift from positive-mean to negative-mean, with the crossover occurring below the quality of current SOTA models.
why_important: Gives practitioners a concrete rule for when to delete a pipeline stage, and demonstrates constructively that method validity is regime-dependent rather than absolute.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: individual observations that CRFs help less on modern models circulate; the regime-boundary characterization (when the sign flips and why) appears uncharted.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply one classical CRF and one learned refiner to outputs of 6 checkpoints spanning old-to-new quality on one benchmark; plot per-image gain distributions against base quality.
main_risk: Refiner hyperparameters tuned per-backbone could mask the flip; the study needs both fixed and re-tuned refiner arms.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Boundary refinement post-processing is a safe, generally positive addition to segmentation pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned refiners trained jointly with strong backbones may adapt and keep a positive mean, confining the negative result to classical CRFs only.
fastest_falsification: Inference-plus-postprocessing sweep over existing checkpoints: about two days, no training.

one_line: Plug-and-play attention modules for segmentation add seed-level noise, not signal, once parameters are matched.
problem: A long line of insert-this-block papers reports 0.5-1.5 mIoU gains; these rarely control for parameter count, FLOPs, and seed variance simultaneously.
core_hypothesis: The median plug-in module gain disappears when the baseline is widened to match parameters/FLOPs and when both arms run 5 seeds; the genre survives on single-seed comparisons against unmatched baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating 6 representative plug-in modules under matched-capacity 5-seed protocols will show median gain below the pooled seed standard deviation on Cityscapes and ADE20K.
why_important: The plug-in genre consumes substantial community attention; a decisive matched-capacity replication would either retire it or identify the rare modules with real effects worth understanding.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: matched-capacity criticism is common folklore; a systematic multi-module segmentation replication with published gain distributions appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One strong baseline, 6 modules, capacity-matched widened baseline control, 5 seeds each, fixed recipe; publish the full gain distribution.
main_risk: Module implementations vary in quality; faithful reimplementation effort is the real cost and a source of dispute.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Well-designed attention/context modules deliver reliable portable gains across segmentation architectures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A minority of modules may show robust matched-capacity gains, converting the study from a debunking into a useful ranking; the null may be too strong.
fastest_falsification: Two modules plus widened control, 3 seeds: one GPU-week for the trend.

one_line: Curriculum ordering of training images does not replicate for segmentation once the LR schedule is re-tuned per arm.
problem: Curriculum strategies (easy-to-hard image ordering, resolution ramps) report gains for dense training, but ordering interacts with learning-rate schedules in ways baselines are rarely allowed to exploit.
core_hypothesis: Curriculum gains are schedule artifacts: any fixed data ordering changes the effective LR-vs-difficulty profile, and re-tuning the baseline schedule with the same budget recovers the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: For 3 published-style curricula, gains over a random-order baseline will drop below 0.3 mIoU once the baseline LR schedule is re-tuned with the identical trial budget the curriculum arm received.
why_important: Curricula add pipeline complexity and hyperparameters; if their effect is absorbable into schedules, the community can simplify training stacks.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: schedule-confound critiques exist for classification curricula; a controlled segmentation-specific replication appears unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement difficulty-scored and resolution-ramp curricula on one benchmark; give baseline and curriculum arms equal schedule-search budgets; 3 seeds.
main_risk: Difficulty scoring itself has degrees of freedom; a strawman difficulty score would unfairly doom the curriculum arm.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Ordering training data from easy to hard measurably improves dense prediction training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Resolution-ramp curricula in particular may deliver genuine compute savings at equal quality, surviving as an efficiency (not accuracy) result.
fastest_falsification: One curriculum vs schedule-tuned baseline, 3 seeds, one dataset: several GPU-days.

one_line: Hard-example mining and class-rebalancing exploit the same slack; combined they add nothing and OHEM alone loses to plain resampling.
problem: Pipelines stack hard-example mining, class-balanced sampling, and weighted losses as if their gains compose; the mechanisms may be redundant corrections of the same imbalance.
core_hypothesis: All three interventions approximate the same reweighting of the empirical risk; whichever is applied first consumes the available gain, and stacking yields no measurable addition while OHEM adds gradient noise that plain resampling avoids.
falsifiable_prediction: A full 2x2x2 factorial (mining x balanced sampling x weighted loss) on two long-tail benchmarks will show interaction terms statistically canceling main effects, with no stack beating the best single intervention by more than 0.2 mIoU.
why_important: Simplifies a bloated part of every practitioner recipe and demonstrates factorial-design evaluation, which the field almost never uses.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: pairwise comparisons exist scattered across papers; a full factorial with interaction analysis for segmentation imbalance tools appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the 8-cell factorial with 3 seeds on one long-tail semantic benchmark and one instance benchmark; fit an ANOVA on mIoU and tail-class IoU.
main_risk: Effects may differ between semantic and instance settings, blurring a single headline conclusion.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Mining, rebalancing, and weighting are complementary tools whose benefits stack for imbalanced segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mining operates per-pixel while rebalancing operates per-image, so the mechanisms could be genuinely orthogonal and the factorial would show additive gains.
fastest_falsification: The 8-cell factorial at reduced schedule length, 2 seeds: one GPU-week for interaction signs.

one_line: Self-distillation gains on segmentation are repackaged schedule and augmentation extensions, not knowledge transfer.
problem: Self-distillation (student learns from same-size teacher trained on the same data) reports free gains for dense tasks; the pipelines quietly grant the student extra effective training (teacher pseudo-labels on augmented views, longer total optimization).
core_hypothesis: Granting the plain baseline the same total compute, augmentation exposure, and label-smoothing effect that the distillation pipeline provides implicitly will close the reported self-distillation gap on segmentation benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: A baseline trained for the combined teacher-plus-student budget with matched augmentation sampling and tuned label smoothing will come within 0.3 mIoU of self-distilled models across 3 architectures.
why_important: Free-lunch claims steer practice; if the lunch is paid by hidden compute, honest accounting changes what teams deploy and what reviewers accept.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compute-matched critiques of distillation exist for classification; segmentation-specific accounting including dense pseudo-label smoothing effects appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms (baseline, compute-matched baseline with smoothing, self-distilled) on two benchmarks, 3 seeds, identical everything else.
main_risk: Label smoothing is an imperfect proxy for dense soft-label structure; the residual gap may be genuinely informative about spatial dark knowledge.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Self-distillation extracts transferable dark knowledge that improves segmentation beyond what the same compute buys directly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spatially structured soft labels may carry boundary-uncertainty information no scalar smoothing replicates, leaving a real residual gain.
fastest_falsification: One architecture, three arms, 3 seeds: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Frequency-domain segmentation modules exploit compression-pipeline artifacts, and their gains vanish on recompression-controlled data.
problem: Wavelet/Fourier feature modules report gains attributed to physics-like frequency reasoning; benchmark images carry dataset-specific JPEG and resize fingerprints those modules can exploit as shortcuts.
core_hypothesis: A meaningful share of frequency-module gains comes from latching onto compression and resampling fingerprints correlated with classes or datasets; re-encoding all splits through a common randomized compression pipeline will erase most of the gain.
falsifiable_prediction: Under randomized recompression applied uniformly to train and test, the mIoU gain of 3 representative frequency modules over matched baselines will drop by more than half relative to original-data evaluation.
why_important: Identifies an unrecognized shortcut channel affecting a whole method genre and yields a cheap hygiene protocol (randomized recompression) for future dense-prediction evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compression shortcuts are documented for forensics and classification; their role in frequency-based segmentation module gains appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrain module and baseline on recompression-randomized versions of two benchmarks; compare gain deltas against original-pipeline training.
main_risk: Recompression also destroys legitimate high-frequency evidence, so a boundary-metric control is needed to separate shortcut removal from information removal.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Frequency-domain modules help because objects have characteristic frequency signatures that spatial convolutions miss.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gains may survive recompression fully, indicating the modules capture genuine spectral structure; the shortcut account would then be falsified cleanly.
fastest_falsification: One module vs baseline on one recompressed benchmark: a few GPU-days including data preparation.

one_line: Pixel-contrastive pretraining does not beat masked-image-modeling for segmentation once pretraining compute is matched.
problem: Dense-contrastive pretraining papers claim superiority for segmentation transfer, but comparisons routinely differ in epochs, batch sizes, and data pipelines from the MIM baselines they quote.
core_hypothesis: At matched pretraining FLOPs, data, and fine-tuning recipe, dense-contrastive and MIM objectives land within noise of each other for segmentation transfer; published orderings reflect compute and recipe asymmetries.
falsifiable_prediction: A matched-compute head-to-head (same backbone, data, FLOPs, fine-tune protocol, 3 seeds) will show the two objective families within 0.4 mIoU on ADE20K and Cityscapes, in whatever direction.
why_important: Pretraining-objective choice drives large compute investments; establishing practical equivalence (or a real ordering) under fair accounting is decision-relevant for anyone training vision backbones.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: fair-comparison studies exist for classification probes; a compute-matched dense-transfer verdict appears unsettled.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain both objectives on identical data at two matched FLOP budgets, fine-tune identically, 3 seeds, report transfer curves.
main_risk: Objective-specific optimal hyperparameters differ; matching compute but not tuning effort could bias either way, so both arms need equal tuning budgets too.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Dense-contrastive objectives are specifically better suited to segmentation transfer than reconstruction objectives.
why_it_might_be_wrong: One family may genuinely dominate at scale; equivalence at small matched budgets might not extrapolate.
fastest_falsification: Small-budget matched pretraining pair plus fine-tuning: about two GPU-weeks total.

one_line: Domain-generalization methods for segmentation stop working once the baseline uses modern strong augmentation.
problem: The DG-for-segmentation literature reports gains over baselines with dated augmentation; strong photometric/geometric augmentation may already occupy the same robustness budget the methods claim.
core_hypothesis: DG method gains and strong-augmentation gains are non-additive because both flatten the same nuisance directions; over an augmentation-modernized baseline, the median DG method gain on unseen-domain mIoU approaches zero.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating 5 representative DG techniques on driving-domain shifts over a strong-augmentation baseline will reduce their median reported gain by at least two thirds.
why_important: Redirects domain-generalization research from method proliferation toward the unsolved residual (structural and content shifts that augmentation cannot mimic).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: baseline-strength critiques are common in DG classification; a systematic segmentation-specific re-baselining appears missing. Flag: territory-adjacent to wave2 worker_A (domain shift), but framed as a non-replication claim rather than a generation-for-segmentation method.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One synthetic-to-real and one real-to-real shift; 5 DG methods over weak and strong baselines; 3 seeds; report gain shrinkage.
main_risk: Some DG methods are themselves augmentation schemes, making the decomposition partly definitional; needs a clear taxonomy before running.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Dedicated domain-generalization machinery adds robustness beyond what standard strong augmentation provides.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Methods operating on features or normalization statistics may target shifts augmentation cannot reach, retaining real gains over any augmentation baseline.
fastest_falsification: Two DG methods over both baselines on one shift: a GPU-week.

one_line: The ImageNet-pretraining crossover for segmentation happens at far smaller dataset sizes than practitioners assume.
problem: Pretraining is treated as mandatory for segmentation at almost any dataset size; the actual crossover where random initialization catches up has not been mapped for modern dense recipes.
core_hypothesis: With modern normalization, augmentation, and longer schedules, random-init segmentation training matches fine-tuned ImageNet pretraining at dataset sizes in the low tens of thousands of densely labeled images, far below community intuition.
falsifiable_prediction: On subsampled dense benchmarks, the pretrain-vs-scratch gap will fall below 0.5 mIoU at a training-set size under 30k images when scratch runs get 3x schedule length.
why_important: Teams with medium proprietary datasets may be paying licensing, contamination, and bias costs of pretrained weights for no accuracy benefit; the crossover map is directly actionable. VERIFIED PRIOR WORK exists for detection-era scratch training; the modern segmentation-specific crossover is the open question.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the scratch-training result is known for older detection setups; a crossover-size map for current segmentation recipes and backbones appears unavailable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train scratch-vs-pretrained pairs at 5 dataset sizes on two benchmarks with schedule compensation for scratch; locate the crossover.
main_risk: Crossover location likely depends on class count and image diversity; a single-benchmark answer may not generalize without at least two domains.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: ImageNet (or larger) pretraining is effectively required for competitive segmentation at all practical dataset sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern transformer backbones may be more pretraining-dependent than the CNNs older scratch results used, pushing the crossover far higher instead.
fastest_falsification: Scratch-vs-pretrained at two dataset sizes on one benchmark: a few GPU-days for the trend direction.

one_line: The SSL-beats-supervised advantage for dense tasks exists only in frozen-feature evaluation, not under full fine-tuning.
problem: The belief that self-supervised pretraining is specifically better for dense prediction rests heavily on frozen or linear evaluations; deployments fine-tune.
core_hypothesis: Full fine-tuning washes out the dense-feature organization SSL provides; at matched pretraining compute and equal fine-tuning tuning budgets, supervised and SSL initializations converge to indistinguishable segmentation performance.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 3 SSL recipes and matched supervised checkpoints, the fine-tuned segmentation gap will be under 0.3 mIoU on two benchmarks despite frozen-probe gaps exceeding 3 points.
why_important: Clarifies what SSL actually buys dense users: cheap adaptation and probing, not final-quality headroom; affects pretraining strategy for dense-focused organizations.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: fine-tune-vs-frozen discrepancies are noted anecdotally; a systematic dense-task equivalence claim under matched budgets appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune matched SSL/supervised checkpoint pairs with equal tuning budgets on two segmentation benchmarks, 3 seeds; compare against their frozen-probe gaps.
main_risk: Truly matched supervised/SSL checkpoint pairs (same data, compute, architecture) are scarce; may require training modest-scale pairs from scratch.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: SSL pretraining produces features intrinsically better for dense downstream tasks than supervised pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On small downstream datasets fine-tuning cannot fully reorganize features, so the SSL edge may persist exactly where users are data-poor.
fastest_falsification: One matched pair, two benchmarks, frozen and fine-tuned arms: a GPU-week.

one_line: Geometry pretraining negatively transfers to semantic boundaries where depth edges and semantic edges disagree.
problem: Depth and geometry pretraining is marketed as broadly beneficial for dense tasks, but semantic boundaries frequently exist without depth discontinuities (markings, material transitions) and vice versa.
core_hypothesis: Depth-pretrained features bias boundary placement toward depth discontinuities, causing systematic errors on flat-but-semantic boundaries; the harm is invisible in mIoU but visible in boundary metrics stratified by boundary type.
falsifiable_prediction: Fine-tuned depth-pretrained models will lose to matched RGB-SSL models on boundary-F over flat semantic boundaries (road markings, wall art, flat signage) by a margin exceeding seed noise, while matching them elsewhere.
why_important: Multi-task and geometry-first pretraining agendas need a documented negative-transfer mode with a diagnostic split, so that pretraining choices can be made per boundary regime.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: negative transfer from depth to semantics has anecdotal mentions; a boundary-type-stratified quantification appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate or auto-derive a flat-vs-depth boundary partition on an existing benchmark; compare matched depth-pretrained vs RGB-pretrained fine-tunes on stratified boundary-F.
main_risk: Automatically classifying boundary types using depth sensors or stereo introduces its own errors; a manual audit subset is required for trust.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Geometry-aware pretraining is at worst neutral and usually helpful for semantic segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuning may fully suppress the depth prior, or depth pretraining may improve flat-boundary contrast sensitivity indirectly, nullifying the stratified gap.
fastest_falsification: Stratified re-scoring of already-released depth-pretrained vs RGB-pretrained segmentation fine-tunes on one dataset: days.

one_line: Linear-probe rankings of backbones do not predict fine-tuned segmentation rankings, breaking the standard cheap selection protocol.
problem: Backbone selection for dense projects is commonly done with frozen linear probes because full fine-tuning is expensive; the implicit rank-preservation assumption is untested for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Frozen-probe segmentation performance and full fine-tuned performance are governed by different backbone properties (feature readability vs adaptability), so cross-backbone rank correlation between the two protocols is weak or absent.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 10+ diverse public backbones, Spearman correlation between linear-probe mIoU and fine-tuned mIoU on the same benchmark will fall below 0.4, with at least two top-3 probe backbones outside the fine-tuned top-5.
why_important: If the cheap protocol misranks, the field is systematically selecting wrong backbones for dense deployments; the result would force honest (more expensive) selection or a corrected cheap proxy.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: probe-vs-finetune rank divergence is studied for classification transfer; a dense-task version across modern backbone families appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe and fine-tune 10 backbones on one benchmark under standardized decoders and budgets; compute rank correlations and top-k overlap.
main_risk: Decoder choice interacts with backbone architecture; a single decoder may unfairly suit some families, requiring a two-decoder control.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Linear-probe performance is an adequate cheap proxy for choosing backbones for dense fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correlation may be high within an architecture family even if weak across families, salvaging the protocol for the common practical case.
fastest_falsification: Probe all 10 cheaply, fine-tune only the probe-top-3 and probe-bottom-3: a focused GPU-week to test rank inversion.

one_line: Foundation-feature generality fails on stuff classes: frozen VFM features are object-biased and lose to older supervised features on amorphous regions.
problem: Frozen vision-foundation-model features are treated as universally strong dense descriptors, but their pretraining (object-centric crops, instance discrimination, promptable masks) may systematically underserve stuff regions like sky, road surface, water, and vegetation texture.
core_hypothesis: Frozen VFM feature probes will show a things-vs-stuff asymmetry: competitive or superior on thing classes, but measurably below supervised ImageNet-era features on stuff classes, because object-centric pretraining allocates capacity to instance boundaries over region texture statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: On ADE20K and COCO-Stuff frozen-probe evaluations, at least two popular VFM feature sets will trail a supervised baseline by 2+ IoU averaged over stuff classes while leading on thing classes.
why_important: Stuff classes dominate pixel area in driving, aerial, and environmental applications; a documented stuff blind spot would change which features practitioners freeze and what pretraining objectives need fixing.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: things-vs-stuff analyses exist for older architectures; a systematic frozen-probe asymmetry study across modern VFM families appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Frozen linear and light-decoder probes for 4 feature families on two stuff-rich benchmarks, with per-class results split by the standard things/stuff partition.
main_risk: Probe architecture choices could mask or exaggerate the asymmetry; needs both linear and small nonlinear probes to be convincing.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Modern foundation features are the best general-purpose dense features for all class types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large VFM training corpora contain abundant scenery, which may have taught stuff statistics implicitly, erasing the predicted asymmetry.
fastest_falsification: Frozen probes only, no backbone training: two days on public checkpoints.

one_line: Intermediate-task segmentation transfer is governed by annotation-protocol match, not semantic similarity.
problem: Transfer pipelines pick intermediate segmentation datasets by semantic closeness to the target; if the transferred asset is mostly protocol style (boundary conventions, granularity), the selection criterion is wrong.
core_hypothesis: A small intermediate dataset with matched annotation protocol will transfer better to a target task than a much larger semantically-closer dataset with mismatched protocol, because models inherit boundary and granularity conventions faster than semantics.
falsifiable_prediction: In a 2x2 design (protocol match x semantic match), protocol-matched small-set transfer will beat semantically-matched large-set transfer on target boundary-F and match it on mIoU.
why_important: Reorders the practical playbook for intermediate fine-tuning and dataset purchasing decisions; protocol becomes a first-class transfer variable.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: protocol effects are discussed in annotation literature; their dominance over semantic similarity in transfer selection appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct the 2x2 by re-annotating a small dataset under the target protocol and using an existing large mismatched-protocol set; fine-tune all four arms into the same target.
main_risk: Confounding semantic and protocol axes cleanly requires careful dataset construction; partial confounds would muddy attribution.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Semantic similarity between intermediate and target tasks is the primary driver of segmentation transfer benefit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For large domain gaps semantics may still dominate; the protocol effect might only matter within-domain, shrinking the claim scope.
fastest_falsification: Run only the two off-diagonal cells (protocol-matched small vs semantic-matched large) into one target: a few GPU-days plus a small annotation effort.

one_line: Frozen-backbone segmentation setups collapse under domain shift much faster than fine-tuned ones, reversing the freeze-is-safe belief.
problem: Freezing foundation backbones and training light decoders is promoted as robust and efficient; robustness under deployment shift has mostly been asserted from in-domain results.
core_hypothesis: Frozen features fix the nuisance-invariance budget at pretraining time; when target-domain nuisances differ (sensor, weather, style), light decoders cannot compensate, so frozen setups lose disproportionately more than end-to-end fine-tuned ones under shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 4 shift pairs, the OOD-minus-ID degradation of frozen-plus-decoder models will exceed that of fully fine-tuned counterparts by at least 50% relative, despite similar ID performance.
why_important: Freeze-vs-tune is one of the most common engineering decisions; a shift-conditioned reversal would rewrite the default advice for deployed dense systems.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: freeze-vs-tune comparisons abound in-domain; shift-stratified degradation accounting for dense tasks appears rare or absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train frozen and fine-tuned variants from identical checkpoints on one source dataset; evaluate both on standard shifted test sets; compare degradation ratios.
main_risk: Fine-tuning may overfit the source domain in ways that also hurt OOD, muddying the comparison; needs multiple source-set sizes.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Frozen foundation features generalize at least as well as fine-tuned ones, and freezing protects against overfitting-induced fragility.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation pretraining may cover deployment nuisances so broadly that frozen features degrade less, confirming rather than refuting the community belief.
fastest_falsification: One source, two shifted targets, frozen-vs-tuned pair: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Video pretraining adds nothing for still-image segmentation once frame counts are matched to image pretraining.
problem: The motion-teaches-objectness narrative motivates expensive video pretraining; comparisons rarely match total frames seen and data diversity against image-only pretraining.
core_hypothesis: For still-image segmentation transfer, temporal structure in pretraining contributes nothing beyond what the same number of diverse frames contributes as independent images; apparent video-pretraining wins are frame-budget and diversity effects.
falsifiable_prediction: Pretraining on shuffled single frames from videos will transfer to image segmentation within 0.3 mIoU of pretraining on the same frames with temporal objectives, across two SSL recipes.
why_important: Video pretraining is much more expensive per useful bit; a null temporal effect for static dense tasks would redirect the video-pretraining agenda toward genuinely temporal targets.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: matched-frame controls appear absent from video-pretraining papers claiming dense-transfer benefits.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two pretraining arms on identical frame sets (temporal objective vs frame-shuffled image objective), identical fine-tuning on two image segmentation benchmarks, 3 seeds.
main_risk: The result may flip for tasks with occlusion reasoning even among still images, requiring careful benchmark selection to keep the claim precise.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Learning from video motion produces better object boundaries and objectness priors that transfer to image segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Temporal correspondence objectives may genuinely sharpen part-whole grouping in ways frame-level objectives cannot, preserving a real gap.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale matched-frame pretraining pair plus one fine-tune benchmark: about a GPU-week.

one_line: Multi-dataset universal segmentation training hides per-dataset regressions caused by taxonomy conflicts.
problem: Universal segmentation models trained across merged datasets report aggregate wins; label-space merging forces contradictory supervision (the same pixel concept labeled differently across sets) whose per-dataset costs are rarely itemized.
core_hypothesis: For a meaningful subset of classes with cross-dataset taxonomy conflicts, joint training performs worse than per-dataset experts, and the aggregate win comes entirely from low-data datasets borrowing capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: Class-level analysis of a jointly trained model vs per-dataset experts will show statistically significant regressions concentrated in classes with documented cross-dataset definition conflicts (for example road vs sidewalk conventions, wall vs fence).
why_important: The universal-model narrative drives dataset consolidation; knowing which classes pay the merger tax enables conflict-aware merging instead of naive unioning.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: taxonomy conflicts are acknowledged as engineering nuisances; a quantified regression accounting attributed to conflicts appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train experts and one joint model on 3 driving/indoor datasets; build a conflict list from label definitions; test whether regression magnitude correlates with conflict membership.
main_risk: Conflict identification is partly subjective; needs two independent annotator-judges to classify conflicts before results are seen.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Training one model across many segmentation datasets is broadly beneficial, with taxonomy issues being minor engineering details.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern language-embedding label spaces may absorb definitional conflicts gracefully, leaving no measurable per-class regressions.
fastest_falsification: Reuse public universal checkpoints and public per-dataset experts, run class-level differencing against a pre-registered conflict list: days, no training.

one_line: Model merging and task arithmetic break down for dense prediction: segmentation task vectors do not compose.
problem: Weight-space merging (adding task vectors, averaging fine-tunes) is reported to work surprisingly well for classification; the community increasingly assumes it transfers to dense tasks.
core_hypothesis: Dense decoders depend on precise cross-layer spatial calibrations that weight averaging destroys nonlinearly; merged segmentation models will lose boundary fidelity catastrophically even when their classification-style region metrics survive.
falsifiable_prediction: Merging two segmentation fine-tunes from a shared initialization will retain over 90% of average mIoU but lose over 30% relative boundary-F on both parent tasks, a dissociation absent in classification merging.
why_important: Model merging promises cheap multi-task deployment; a documented dense-task failure mode with a metric signature would prevent silent quality loss in production merges.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: merging papers evaluate classification and occasionally detection; boundary-stratified segmentation merging analysis appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one backbone on two segmentation datasets, merge with 3 published weight-space recipes, evaluate region and boundary metrics against both parents.
main_risk: Result may depend on decoder architecture; query-based and per-pixel decoders may fail differently, requiring both to be tested.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Weight-space task arithmetic is a general phenomenon that extends to dense prediction models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-initialization fine-tunes may stay in a linearly connected basin where dense calibrations survive averaging, making merging just work.
fastest_falsification: Two fine-tunes plus three merges plus evaluation: a few GPU-days total.

one_line: Lp-adversarial training for segmentation buys almost no protection against physically realizable attacks.
problem: Robust segmentation research optimizes Lp-ball robustness; deployed threats are patches, stickers, textures, and lighting manipulations that live far outside small Lp balls.
core_hypothesis: Lp-robust segmentation models retain near-baseline vulnerability to physically realizable attacks because the two threat models exercise almost disjoint failure circuits; Lp robustness is a poor proxy investment.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 3 Lp-adversarially-trained segmenters, printed-patch and projected-light attacks will degrade target-region IoU by at least 80% as much as they degrade standard models, despite large measured Lp-robustness gaps.
why_important: Safety cases for perception systems cite adversarial training; quantifying the proxy failure redirects effort toward threat-model-faithful defenses.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: proxy-gap observations exist for classification; a systematic physical-vs-Lp transfer matrix for dense prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public robust and standard segmentation checkpoints, run one patch attack and one light/color-field attack in simulation plus a small physical validation, compare degradation ratios.
main_risk: Physical attack reproducibility is finicky; simulation-to-physical agreement must be spot-checked to keep the claim credible.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Adversarial training meaningfully hardens segmentation models against real-world adversaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Lp training may confer partial gradient-smoothness benefits that measurably blunt patch optimization, yielding moderate rather than near-zero protection.
fastest_falsification: Simulation-only patch attack on two checkpoint pairs: days, public code paths exist for both attack styles.

one_line: Published robust-segmentation numbers are inflated by gradient masking; dense-aware adaptive attacks will halve them.
problem: Segmentation defenses are typically evaluated with attacks ported from classification that optimize a summed per-pixel loss, which is prone to gradient dilution and masking artifacts specific to dense outputs.
core_hypothesis: Attacks that adaptively select pixel subsets, rebalance per-pixel gradients, and target structural metrics will reveal that a large fraction of claimed robust-mIoU across defense families is evaluation artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: A dense-aware adaptive attack suite will reduce reported robust mIoU by more than 40% relative on at least half of a sample of published segmentation defenses, while leaving properly-evaluated baselines unchanged.
why_important: Robustness numbers feed safety documentation; a field-wide overestimate is a correctable systemic error, and the attack suite is a constructive reusable artifact.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: adaptive-attack re-evaluations transformed classification robustness; an equivalent dense-prediction re-evaluation appears not to have been done at scale.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement pixel-subset and gradient-rebalanced PGD variants, re-evaluate 6 public defense checkpoints, report before/after robust-metric tables.
main_risk: Defense reimplementation fidelity disputes; must use released checkpoints only and publish full attack code.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Reported robust-segmentation gains reflect genuine robustness rather than evaluation weaknesses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense outputs may actually make gradient masking harder (many loss terms provide signal), so the inflation could be small and the field healthier than classification was.
fastest_falsification: Run the strongest existing attack with per-pixel gradient renormalization on 3 public defense checkpoints: a few days.

one_line: Certified segmentation robustness certifies the easy pixels: interiors get certificates, boundaries never do.
problem: Randomized-smoothing certificates are being extended to segmentation, and headline certified-pixel percentages look encouraging without spatial analysis of which pixels get certified.
core_hypothesis: Certified pixels concentrate in large-region interiors that were never at risk, while boundary-band pixels (the operationally critical ones) receive vanishing certified radii, making headline certified percentages practically vacuous.
falsifiable_prediction: For public certified-segmentation methods, over 90% of certified pixels will lie outside a 10-pixel boundary band, and certified fraction inside the band will be under 10%, on standard benchmarks.
why_important: Prevents a false sense of security from certification papers and defines the actual open problem: certifying decision-relevant boundary regions; constructive follow-up is a boundary-weighted certification objective.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: spatial stratification of dense certificates appears unreported; papers publish aggregate certified percentages.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-run released certification code on two benchmarks, stratify certified radii by distance-to-boundary, publish the spatial profile.
main_risk: Mostly analysis of existing artifacts; the risk is that the field considers the finding obvious-in-hindsight without the constructive follow-up attached.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Certified-pixel percentages meaningfully summarize how protected a segmentation model is.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some certified methods with shape priors may certify boundary bands better than expected, weakening the vacuity claim.
fastest_falsification: Stratified re-analysis of released certification outputs: one or two days.

one_line: Black-box transferability of segmentation attacks is far weaker than the classification-derived threat narrative claims.
problem: Threat assessments assume adversarial examples transfer across architectures as readily for dense models as for classifiers, justifying black-box alarm; dense attack transfer may actually be fragile.
core_hypothesis: Dense attacks overfit the surrogate's spatial feature geometry; cross-architecture transfer of segmentation attacks degrades much faster than classification attack transfer at matched perturbation budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: In a transfer matrix over 5 architectures, off-diagonal segmentation attack success (target-region IoU drop) will average under 30% of on-diagonal success, versus classification transfer ratios historically reported far higher; the classification comparison arm will be reproduced, not quoted.
why_important: Right-sizes the black-box threat model for perception systems and shifts defensive priorities toward query-based and physical threats where exposure is real.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: transfer studies exist for detection sporadically; a systematic dense-prediction transfer matrix with matched-budget classification control appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate attacks on each of 5 segmenters, evaluate all 25 pairs, run an identical-protocol classification transfer matrix as control, compare off-diagonal ratios.
main_risk: Attack strength choices dominate transfer numbers; requires multiple budgets and attack families to avoid strawman transfer.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Adversarial examples transfer well across models, so black-box adversaries are nearly as dangerous as white-box ones for dense perception.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared pretrained backbones across modern segmenters may create strong transfer channels, making dense transfer as good or better than classification transfer.
fastest_falsification: A 3x3 sub-matrix with one attack family: two days on public checkpoints.

one_line: The robustness-accuracy tradeoff in segmentation is an artifact of importing classification epsilon budgets.
problem: Robust segmentation training uses perturbation budgets copied from classification benchmarks; dense outputs may tolerate per-pixel budgets differently, manufacturing an apparent clean-accuracy sacrifice.
core_hypothesis: With perturbation budgets calibrated to dense-output sensitivity (smaller or spatially weighted epsilon), adversarial training yields robustness gains with negligible clean-mIoU loss; the reported tradeoff reflects mis-scaled threat budgets, not a fundamental tension.
falsifiable_prediction: An epsilon sweep will reveal a regime where robust training recovers over 80% of the standard robustness gain while losing under 0.5 clean mIoU, a point excluded by default classification-derived budgets.
why_important: The perceived clean-accuracy tax is the main reason practitioners skip robust training for dense models; removing it changes deployment defaults.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: epsilon-sensitivity analyses exist for classification; dense-calibrated budget studies appear rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Adversarially train one segmenter across 5 epsilon values and one spatially-weighted variant; map the clean-vs-robust frontier and locate the predicted regime.
main_risk: The favorable regime may deliver robustness only against small perturbations nobody cares about, making the result technically true but operationally empty.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Robustness necessarily costs clean segmentation accuracy, as established in classification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The tradeoff may be intrinsic to feature smoothing regardless of budget scaling, in which case the frontier shows no free-lunch regime.
fastest_falsification: Three-point epsilon sweep on one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Synthetic corruption benchmarks do not predict real acquisition-degradation robustness for segmentation.
problem: Corruption suites (synthetic fog, blur, noise) are used as proxies for real-world robustness; models and methods are being selected on these proxies without validation against genuinely degraded captures.
core_hypothesis: Rank correlation between synthetic-corruption robustness and robustness on real degraded imagery (real fog, night, rain, motion blur from actual sensors) is weak for modern segmenters because synthetic corruptions miss the joint statistics of real degradation.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 10+ public segmentation models, Spearman correlation between corruption-suite mIoU retention and real-degradation mIoU retention will fall below 0.5 for at least two of four degradation types.
why_important: If the proxy misranks, years of robustness method selection may be misdirected; a validated real-degradation evaluation battery becomes the constructive deliverable.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: synthetic-vs-real robustness gaps are shown for classification weather corruptions; a model-ranking correlation study for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a model zoo on a corruption suite and on real paired-degradation datasets (clear/foggy, day/night driving sets); compute retention rank correlations per degradation type.
main_risk: Real degraded datasets also shift content (different scenes at night), confounding degradation with distribution shift; paired or geo-aligned subsets are needed.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Synthetic corruption benchmarks are adequate proxies for real-world segmentation robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correlations may be high for photometric degradations even if weak for weather, partially validating the proxy and demanding a nuanced verdict.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only evaluation of public checkpoints on existing real and synthetic degraded sets: days.

one_line: Single-frame adversarial patch alarm is overstated: trivial temporal aggregation collapses patch attack success on video segmentation.
problem: Patch-attack papers demonstrate dramatic single-frame segmentation failures, implying deployed video systems are equally exposed; deployed systems aggregate over time.
core_hypothesis: Patch attacks optimized per-frame are brittle to viewpoint and temporal jitter; simple majority voting or exponential smoothing over 5-10 frames restores most of the attacked region IoU without any dedicated defense.
falsifiable_prediction: Under realistic video with egomotion, 5-frame temporal voting will recover at least 70% of the IoU destroyed by published-style patches, while costing under 1 mIoU on clean video.
why_important: Threat-model right-sizing: if free temporal aggregation neutralizes the demonstrated attacks, the real research problem is temporally robust attacks and defenses, not single-frame showpieces.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: temporal-defense observations exist for detection tracking; a quantified aggregation-vs-patch study for dense segmentation appears missing.
