minimal_falsification_experiment: Optimize patches against a video segmenter per published recipes, replay attacks in short driving clips, compare attacked IoU with and without temporal voting.
main_risk: Attacks re-optimized against the aggregation (expectation-over-time attacks) may defeat it; the claim must be scoped to attacks as published.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Demonstrated patch attacks on segmentation imply comparable vulnerability in deployed video pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Patches physically present in the scene persist across frames, so temporal consistency may reinforce rather than average out the attack.
fastest_falsification: Replay one public patch attack over clips with and without voting: two days.

one_line: Strong data augmentation delivers most of adversarial training's robustness for segmentation at a fraction of the cost.
problem: Adversarial training is the default robustness recipe despite 3-10x training cost; the marginal robustness it adds over modern aggressive augmentation has not been isolated for dense tasks.
core_hypothesis: A large share of dense-task robustness attributed to adversarial training is generic input-smoothness regularization that strong photometric-geometric-mixing augmentation also provides; the AT-specific increment is small except at large perturbation budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Strong-augmentation training will close at least 60% of the robust-mIoU gap between vanilla and adversarially trained segmenters at small-to-medium attack budgets, at no extra training cost over standard recipes.
why_important: If augmentation covers most practical robustness, resource-constrained teams get a defensible cheap recipe, and AT research must justify itself on the specific residual.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: augmentation-vs-AT decompositions exist partially for classification; a budget-stratified segmentation version appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train vanilla, strong-aug, and AT variants of one segmenter; evaluate across attack budgets; report the closure fraction per budget.
main_risk: Closure fraction may collapse at exactly the budgets attackers would use, making the cheap recipe a false economy.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Adversarial training provides robustness that data augmentation fundamentally cannot.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gradient-aligned perturbations exploit directions augmentation never samples, so the closure fraction could be small at all budgets.
fastest_falsification: Three training runs and one attack sweep on one benchmark: about a GPU-week.

one_line: Dense supervision is an implicit adversarial regularizer: segmenters are naturally harder to fully break than classifiers on the same backbone.
problem: The community ports the extreme-fragility narrative from classification to dense prediction without measuring whether dense output structure changes the attack economics.
core_hypothesis: Because an attacker must coordinate thousands of coupled output decisions, driving a segmenter to near-total failure requires substantially more perturbation energy than driving a same-backbone classifier to total failure; partial local attacks remain easy but global collapse is expensive.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched backbones, the perturbation norm needed to reduce segmentation to near-chance over the full image will exceed the norm for classifier total failure by at least 3x, while small-region attacks remain cheap.
why_important: Recalibrates threat models: global stealth attacks may be impractical, focusing defense where attacks are actually cheap (local, targeted regions); constructive outcome is an attack-cost map over spatial extent.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-task attack-cost comparisons at matched backbones appear unreported; fragility is usually asserted qualitatively.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Attack a shared-backbone classifier and segmenter with identical PGD machinery; sweep target extent from 1% to 100% of pixels; plot required-norm versus extent curves.
main_risk: Defining near-chance for segmentation needs care (predicting all-background is not chance); metric choices could be contested.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Segmentation models are as trivially breakable as classifiers; dense outputs offer no intrinsic resistance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spatial correlation of features may let single perturbation patterns flip huge regions cheaply, collapsing the predicted 3x separation.
fastest_falsification: Extent-sweep attack on one backbone pair: two days.

one_line: Adversarial-input detectors ported to segmentation fail against region-targeted attacks that leave global statistics untouched.
problem: Detection-based defenses flag adversarial inputs via logit or feature statistics; dense attacks need not perturb global statistics at all if they target small regions (a pedestrian, a sign).
core_hypothesis: Published detector families tuned on whole-image attacks will drop to near-chance detection against attacks confined to small semantically critical regions, because the detectors integrate evidence over the entire image.
falsifiable_prediction: Detector AUROC will fall below 0.6 for attacks perturbing under 5% of pixels while those same attacks eliminate the target object from predictions.
why_important: The most dangerous dense attacks are precisely the local ones; showing the detector genre is blind to them defines the actual open problem (spatially localized detection).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: localized-attack blind spots are plausible from first principles but appear unmeasured for segmentation detector defenses.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce two detector defenses on a segmenter, evaluate against whole-image and region-confined PGD variants, report AUROC by perturbed-area fraction.
main_risk: Constructing fair region-confined attacks with matched per-pixel budgets requires care to avoid trivially stronger local perturbations.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Adversarial-input detection transfers naturally from classification to dense prediction pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Local attacks may still leave detectable feature anomalies at the attacked location that patch-level detectors catch, refuting the blindness claim.
fastest_falsification: One detector, two attack extents: two or three days.

one_line: Robustness is dataset-idiosyncratic: adversarially robust segmentation backbones do not stay robust after fine-tuning elsewhere.
problem: The community increasingly treats robust backbones as reusable artifacts (train robust once, fine-tune anywhere robustly); robustness may not survive dense fine-tuning across datasets.
core_hypothesis: Adversarial robustness lives substantially in dataset-specific decision geometry rather than backbone features; fine-tuning a robust backbone on a new segmentation dataset without adversarial training will forfeit most robustness even though clean accuracy transfers.
falsifiable_prediction: Robust-pretrained backbones fine-tuned conventionally on a second dataset will retain under 30% of their robust-mIoU advantage over standard backbones, while retaining over 80% of any clean-accuracy advantage.
why_important: Kills or validates the robust-backbone-as-infrastructure business case; if robustness must be re-earned per dataset, cost models for safe perception change completely.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: robustness transfer studies exist for classification with mixed results; a dense-task fine-tuning-forgetting quantification appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune robust and standard checkpoints on two new segmentation datasets with identical recipes; attack all variants; compare retained robustness fractions.
main_risk: Retention may depend on fine-tuning length and learning rate, requiring a small sweep to make the claim robust.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Robust pretrained backbones transfer their robustness to downstream dense tasks like they transfer accuracy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Robust features (smoother, lower-frequency) may be architecture-level properties that survive any fine-tuning, yielding high retention.
fastest_falsification: One robust/standard pair, one downstream dataset, one attack: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Promptable segmentation robustness numbers are inflated because evaluations attack per-prompt instead of prompt-agnostically.
problem: Robustness evaluations of promptable segmenters attack a fixed prompt; real adversaries perturb the image once and must defeat whatever prompts users issue, but defenders also only report the per-prompt setting, which understates transferable image-space weaknesses.
core_hypothesis: Prompt-agnostic attacks on the image encoder (perturbing shared features rather than prompt-conditioned outputs) will simultaneously defeat most prompts at once, revealing that promptable models have a single point of failure the per-prompt evaluation hides.
falsifiable_prediction: An encoder-feature-space attack will reduce mean mask IoU across 50 random prompts by at least 70% of what per-prompt attacks achieve individually, at the same perturbation budget, demonstrating one-perturbation-fits-all-prompts vulnerability.
why_important: Promptable foundation segmenters are becoming annotation and perception infrastructure; a shared-encoder single point of failure changes how their robustness should be evaluated and defended.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: encoder-level attacks on promptable models have started appearing; a systematic prompt-agnostic vs per-prompt inflation quantification appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Attack encoder features of a public promptable segmenter, evaluate mask quality over a prompt battery, compare with per-prompt attack results at matched budget.
main_risk: Feature-space attack strength depends on layer choice; a weak layer choice would understate the vulnerability and falsely acquit the evaluation practice.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Per-prompt attack evaluations adequately characterize promptable-segmenter robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prompt-conditioned decoding may re-route around damaged features per prompt, making prompt-agnostic attacks fundamentally weaker and the current evaluation roughly fair.
fastest_falsification: One encoder attack vs per-prompt attack battery on a public checkpoint: two or three days.

one_line: Skin-tone segmentation gaps are mostly photometric, not representational: luminance-matched evaluation erases the majority of the gap.
problem: Performance gaps across skin tones in human segmentation and portrait matting are attributed to dataset representation imbalance, driving data-collection remedies that may target the wrong variable.
core_hypothesis: The dominant share of measured skin-tone gaps traces to exposure, contrast, and illumination statistics correlated with skin tone in typical photography, not to identity-linked feature deficits; controlling image photometry removes most of the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: After histogram/exposure matching or controlled relighting, cross-skin-tone IoU gaps on human parsing will shrink by over 60%, while dataset rebalancing at fixed photometry shrinks them by under 20%.
why_important: Remedy selection: if photometry dominates, capture-pipeline and augmentation fixes are cheap and effective while costly data rebalancing underdelivers; this redirects fairness engineering.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: photometric confounds are acknowledged in face recognition literature; a controlled decomposition for dense human segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a relighting-capable portrait dataset or controlled capture set; evaluate parsing models across tones under matched vs natural photometry; decompose the gap.
main_risk: Relighting methods may themselves have tone-dependent quality, contaminating the control; physical controlled captures may be needed for the definitive version.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Skin-tone performance gaps primarily reflect training-data representation imbalance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Residual gaps after photometric control may stay large, confirming representational causes and refuting the photometric account.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate existing parsing models on an existing multi-illumination face/body dataset stratified by tone: days, no training.

one_line: Group-balancing training data fails to close segmentation gaps because the gaps live in annotation quality, not sample counts.
problem: Dataset rebalancing is the default fairness intervention; if per-group annotation quality differs (boundary care, ambiguity resolution), balanced counts cannot close performance gaps.
core_hypothesis: For several demographic and content groups, ground-truth mask quality differs systematically (annotator familiarity, hair/garment conventions); models learn and are scored against these quality differences, so balancing counts leaves gaps intact.
falsifiable_prediction: Exact count-balancing will close under 25% of measured gaps, while re-annotating the lower-quality group's labels under a unified protocol closes over 60%, on at least one human-parsing and one general benchmark.
why_important: Redirects fairness budgets from collection to annotation quality control, and reframes some model bias findings as measurement bias; constructive deliverable is a per-group annotation-quality assay.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: label-quality disparities are documented in isolated audits; their quantitative share of segmentation performance gaps appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick one benchmark with measurable group gaps; run count-balancing and unified-protocol re-annotation arms; compare gap closure per intervention.
main_risk: Re-annotation is expensive and its protocol choices could be accused of tilting the result; requires pre-registered protocol and blinded annotators.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Balancing group representation in training data is the primary lever for closing group performance gaps.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For some groups the gap may indeed be sample-count driven, and balancing could close most of it, restoring the standard remedy.
fastest_falsification: Re-annotate 200 images for the worst-gap group under the unified protocol and re-score existing models: annotation-bounded, small compute.

one_line: Classification-born fairness interventions equalize image-level metrics while worsening boundary-level disparities in dense prediction.
problem: Reweighting and adversarial-debiasing methods are transplanted from classification to segmentation with fairness measured on image-level or region-level aggregates, potentially hiding spatial redistribution of errors.
core_hypothesis: These interventions rebalance coarse error totals by sacrificing boundary precision on the protected group (models hedge with blobby masks), so region-metric gaps close while boundary-metric gaps widen; fairness is claimed on the metric that improved.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying two standard debiasing methods to human segmentation will reduce the group mIoU gap while increasing the group boundary-F gap by a comparable relative amount on the same test sets.
why_important: Boundary quality drives downstream harms in portrait editing, medical margins, and AR; a metric-shell-game finding forces dense-specific fairness criteria.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: multi-metric fairness accounting for dense tasks appears essentially absent; interventions are imported and scored on single aggregates.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train baseline and two debiased variants on one human-centric benchmark; report group gaps under region and boundary metrics simultaneously.
main_risk: Boundary-metric noise is higher, requiring more seeds to establish the widening effect confidently.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Fairness interventions that close measured group gaps improve fairness overall for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interventions might close both metric families together, showing they generalize across error types and acquitting the transplant practice.
fastest_falsification: One debiasing method, one dataset, dual-metric reporting, 3 seeds: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Geographic segmentation gaps are scene-composition effects, not appearance effects: models fail on unfamiliar layouts, not unfamiliar objects.
problem: Cross-region performance gaps (models trained on western imagery underperforming elsewhere) are commonly attributed to object-appearance differences, motivating appearance-diverse data collection.
core_hypothesis: The dominant gap driver is scene composition and context statistics (object co-occurrence, density, layout, viewpoint), so appearance-focused data fixes underdeliver; layout-matched evaluation removes most of the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying cross-region test sets by scene-layout similarity to training data will explain over 60% of the measured mIoU gap, while object-crop evaluation (classification of same objects without context) shows small cross-region differences.
why_important: Redirects geographic-fairness data investment from photographing more object variants toward covering scene structures, and changes how region-transfer benchmarks should be constructed.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: context-vs-appearance decompositions exist for object recognition; a layout-stratified accounting of geographic dense-prediction gaps appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use geographically diverse benchmarks; compute layout descriptors; regress per-image performance gaps on layout-vs-appearance similarity; add object-crop control probes.
main_risk: Layout and appearance similarity correlate; disentanglement needs careful matched subsets and may leave a contested residual.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Geographic gaps mainly reflect unfamiliar object appearances that more diverse object imagery would fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For some categories (stoves, signage, vehicles) appearance shift is genuinely large, and crop probes may reveal big appearance-driven deficits after all.
fastest_falsification: Re-analysis of existing cross-region evaluations with layout descriptors and crop probes: mostly analysis, days of compute.

one_line: Reported demographic gaps in human parsing can flip sign under alternative reasonable annotation conventions.
problem: Gap measurements assume ground truth is convention-free; hair extent, garment inclusion, and skin-boundary conventions differ across plausible protocols and may interact with group appearance differently.
core_hypothesis: For some group comparisons, the measured direction of the parsing gap depends on annotation convention choices (for example whether voluminous hairstyles are included fully), so published gap tables partly encode protocol interaction effects rather than model bias.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating one benchmark subset under two documented conventions will flip the sign or eliminate significance of at least one commonly cited group gap, while leaving other gaps stable.
why_important: Fairness claims feed policy and product decisions; convention-sensitivity analysis must become standard before gaps are attributed to models. Constructive deliverable: a convention-robust gap estimator reporting ranges over protocols.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation-convention sensitivity of fairness metrics appears unstudied for dense human parsing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-convention re-annotation of 300 images spanning groups; re-score public parsing models; report gap estimates per convention with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Choosing conventions post-hoc invites bias accusations; both conventions must be pre-registered from existing published protocol documents.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Measured group gaps reflect model behavior; ground-truth conventions are neutral infrastructure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gaps may prove convention-invariant, strengthening the standard interpretation and reducing this to a useful robustness check.
fastest_falsification: 300-image dual-convention re-annotation plus re-scoring: annotation-bounded, roughly one week end to end.

one_line: Worst-group-optimizing training makes the worst group worse on clean re-annotated ground truth by overfitting its label noise.
problem: Distributionally robust optimization and group-weighted training are adopted to protect minority groups; minority groups often have noisier labels, which worst-group losses amplify.
core_hypothesis: When per-group label noise is unequal, minimax-style training chases noise in the smallest noisy group; measured on carefully re-annotated clean test data, worst-group segmentation quality decreases relative to standard training.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark with induced or documented group-noise asymmetry, DRO-style training will improve worst-group metrics on original test labels but degrade them by a significant margin on cleaned test labels, versus ERM.
why_important: A fairness method that helps on paper and harms in reality is the worst failure mode; the noise-interaction mechanism gives a concrete precondition to check before deploying group-robust losses.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: DRO-noise interactions are studied for classification; the dense-prediction version with re-annotated evaluation appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct group-asymmetric label noise on a parsing benchmark (or use a naturally noisy group), train ERM and two group-robust methods, evaluate on original and cleaned test labels.
main_risk: Synthetic noise may not mimic real annotation failure structure; a companion natural-noise arm is needed for external validity.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Group-robust objectives reliably improve outcomes for the disadvantaged group.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regularized DRO variants may resist noise amplification, keeping worst-group gains real even under asymmetric noise.
fastest_falsification: One noise-asymmetric setup, ERM vs one DRO variant, cleaned 200-image test subset: a few GPU-days plus modest annotation.

one_line: Clothing contrast dwarfs demographic attributes as the driver of pedestrian segmentation failure, but only demographics get measured.
problem: Fairness audits of pedestrian perception stratify by demographic attributes; photometric factors like clothing-background contrast may dominate risk and remain unreported because they are not protected attributes.
core_hypothesis: Variance in pedestrian segmentation quality explained by clothing-contrast and illumination factors exceeds variance explained by demographic attributes by a large factor; safety-relevant blind spots are photometric, and demographic gap findings partly proxy for clothing statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: A variance decomposition over a pedestrian benchmark will attribute at least 3x more segmentation-quality variance to contrast/illumination covariates than to demographic covariates, and controlling contrast will shrink measured demographic gaps substantially.
why_important: Safety engineering should target the causally dominant variable; if that is contrast, interventions (sensor, HDR, augmentation) differ completely from demographic-data remedies, while fairness reporting should add photometric controls.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: contrast effects are known qualitatively in detection; a formal variance decomposition against demographic attributes for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate contrast and illumination covariates on an existing demographically annotated pedestrian set; fit mixed-effects models of per-instance IoU; report variance shares.
main_risk: Covariates are correlated (clothing styles vary across groups), so causal language must stay careful; matched-subset analysis is required alongside regression.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Demographic attributes are the primary fairness axis to audit in pedestrian perception.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Demographic variance may remain large after photometric control (for example via dataset representation effects), keeping identity-first auditing justified.
fastest_falsification: Covariate annotation on 1000 existing instances plus regression on existing model outputs: about a week, mostly annotation.

one_line: Face-blurring training data costs segmentation models almost nothing, contradicting the raw-data-retention argument.
problem: Organizations resist privacy-preserving anonymization of training imagery on the belief that blurring faces and plates degrades downstream dense models; the belief is largely untested for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Faces and plates occupy tiny pixel fractions and contribute negligible training signal for general segmentation classes; models trained on anonymized data will match raw-data models within noise except on the blurred classes themselves.
falsifiable_prediction: Training on face/plate-blurred versions of two benchmarks will change overall mIoU by under 0.2 and person-class IoU by under 0.5, across 3 seeds.
why_important: Removes a false technical excuse against privacy-preserving practice; a clean null result here has direct policy value for dataset governance.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: anonymization-impact studies exist for detection and driving datasets in places; a systematic segmentation-focused null test with seed statistics appears worth pinning down. VERIFIED PRIOR WORK may partially exist; the replication and boundary conditions are the contribution.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Blur faces/plates with an off-the-shelf detector pipeline on two datasets; train matched models on raw vs anonymized data; compare per-class metrics.
main_risk: If detection-based blurring misses or over-blurs regions systematically, effects could be pipeline artifacts rather than anonymization effects; needs blur-quality audit.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Anonymizing training imagery measurably degrades dense model quality, justifying raw-data retention.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Person-heavy tasks (parsing, crowd scenes) may genuinely suffer from face blurring, limiting the null to non-person-centric segmentation.
fastest_falsification: One dataset, raw-vs-blurred training pair, 3 seeds: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Most published fairness-accuracy tradeoff points for dense models are statistically indistinguishable: the tradeoff is underpowered, not established.
problem: Papers plot fairness-accuracy tradeoffs from single runs on small per-group test subsets; per-group sample sizes for dense metrics may be far too small to support the claimed orderings.
core_hypothesis: Accounting for per-group metric variance (bootstrap over images and seeds), a large fraction of published-style tradeoff comparisons cannot reject the null of no tradeoff; the community narrative rests on underpowered evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running 4 debiasing methods with 5 seeds and bootstrap CIs will show that in the majority of method-vs-baseline comparisons, the claimed accuracy cost or fairness gain (or both) lies inside the joint confidence region of zero effect.
why_important: Constructive outcome is a power-analysis standard for fairness evaluations (minimum group test sizes, seed counts) that would make future tradeoff claims meaningful.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: power critiques exist in fairness classification literature; dense-prediction fairness evaluations with formal power analysis appear absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce a small set of debiasing methods on one benchmark with proper seed replication and bootstrap; publish effect sizes with CIs and the implied minimum sample sizes.
main_risk: Reproduction fidelity disputes; mitigate by using released code and checkpoints where available.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: The fairness-accuracy tradeoff in dense prediction is empirically established by existing comparisons.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some tradeoffs may be large enough to survive proper statistics, converting the critique into confirmation with better error bars.
fastest_falsification: Bootstrap re-analysis of any released per-image results, before any retraining: days.

one_line: Demographic gaps in medical segmentation are mostly scanner and site confounds, not patient-attribute effects.
problem: Reported performance gaps across patient demographics in medical segmentation drive concern about biased models; demographic composition varies strongly across acquisition sites and scanner types, which independently drive performance.
core_hypothesis: Within-scanner, within-site stratified evaluation will erase the majority of measured demographic gaps in organ/tumor segmentation, indicating the gaps are acquisition confounds mislabeled as demographic bias.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-site public medical benchmarks, demographic gaps computed within scanner-site strata will be under 40% of the naive pooled gaps for most organ tasks.
why_important: Misattributed bias leads to wrong fixes (demographic data collection instead of harmonization); site-stratified reporting should become the required control. Flag: adjacent to wave-1 worker_B medical territory, but this is a contrarian measurement claim, not a segmentation method.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: scanner confounding is well known in radiomics; its quantitative share of published demographic segmentation gaps appears unassessed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reanalyze public multi-site segmentation datasets with demographic metadata; compare pooled vs stratified gap estimates with hierarchical models.
main_risk: Stratification can over-control if scanner assignment is itself demographically structured for care-access reasons; requires causal-diagram transparency.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Measured demographic gaps in medical segmentation reflect model bias against patient groups.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some gaps may persist fully within strata (anatomy or disease-presentation differences), validating the demographic-bias reading for those tasks.
fastest_falsification: Pure reanalysis of existing predictions on multi-site sets with metadata: days, no training.

one_line: Generative rebalancing backfires: synthetic minority-group images degrade minority-group segmentation because generators are worse for those groups.
problem: Teams patch representation gaps by generating synthetic images of underrepresented groups; generative models trained on the same skewed distributions may render those groups with lower fidelity, feeding distorted training signal exactly where data was scarce.
core_hypothesis: Generator fidelity is group-dependent in the same direction as the original imbalance, so synthetic augmentation injects systematic appearance and boundary artifacts for minority groups; downstream group gaps widen or stay flat rather than close.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetic-rebalanced training will fail to improve minority-group IoU beyond noise while measurably increasing artifact-correlated failure modes, whereas equal-count real-data addition improves it, on at least one human-centric benchmark.
why_important: Synthetic rebalancing is becoming default practice; a documented backfire mechanism with a fidelity-audit precondition would prevent harm and set a usage standard. Flag: adjacent to wave-2 worker_A synthetic-data territory; framed here strictly as a fairness-backfire claim.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: generator quality disparities are documented for face generation; the downstream dense-task backfire loop appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare three training arms (baseline, synthetic-rebalanced, real-rebalanced with matched counts) on group-stratified segmentation metrics; audit generator fidelity per group first.
main_risk: Access to matched real minority-group data for the control arm is the practical bottleneck; without it the comparison loses its anchor.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Generating synthetic data for underrepresented groups reliably improves their downstream performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern generators may be uniformly high-fidelity across groups, or segmentation may be insensitive to residual generation artifacts, making rebalancing genuinely work.
fastest_falsification: Fidelity audit of one public generator across groups plus a single rebalanced fine-tune: about a week.

one_line: Test-set composition moves measured group gaps more than model interventions do: the bias is in the benchmark, not the model.
problem: Fairness progress is tracked by gap metrics on fixed test sets whose group-conditional difficulty composition (pose, occlusion, scale distributions per group) is uncontrolled and may dominate measured gaps.
core_hypothesis: Resampling test sets to match difficulty covariates across groups changes measured gaps by more than typical published intervention effects; many model-bias rankings are benchmark-composition rankings.
falsifiable_prediction: Difficulty-matched resampling of two fairness benchmarks will change group gap magnitudes by over 50% relative for most evaluated models, exceeding the median published intervention effect on the same benchmarks.
why_important: Constructive deliverable is covariate-matched gap estimation as a reporting standard; without it, intervention comparisons are noise. This reframes part of the fairness literature as benchmark measurement error.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: covariate-matching critiques exist in face recognition evaluation; dense-prediction fairness benchmarks appear not to have been stress-tested this way.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate difficulty covariates (occlusion, scale, blur) on two group-labeled benchmarks; compare naive vs matched gap estimates across a model zoo; compare deltas to published intervention effects.
main_risk: Difficulty covariates are partly group-constitutive (occlusion styles differ by context); over-matching could erase real disparities, so both estimates must be reported side by side.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Group gap metrics on standard benchmarks measure model bias with enough fidelity to rank interventions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gaps may prove composition-stable, validating existing benchmarks and confining the critique to a due-diligence check.
fastest_falsification: Covariate annotation of 500 images per group on one benchmark plus re-scoring existing models: about a week, mostly annotation.

one_line: Fixing existing label errors beats collecting new images per annotation-hour, up to surprisingly large dataset sizes.
problem: Data budgets default to growth (more images) rather than repair (fix masks already collected); the marginal value comparison has never been made under honest hourly accounting for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Training-label errors impose a persistent quality ceiling; below a large dataset-size threshold, an hour spent correcting worst-offender masks yields more test-set gain than an hour spent labeling new images.
falsifiable_prediction: On two mid-size benchmarks, a repair pipeline (model-disagreement-ranked mask correction) will beat new-image collection by at least 2x mIoU gain per annotation-hour at dataset sizes up to tens of thousands of images.
why_important: Reverses the default data strategy for most applied teams and provides an operational repair-vs-grow decision rule based on measurable disagreement statistics.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: label-error effects and relabeling case studies exist; a controlled per-hour marginal-value comparison against collection appears missing for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix total annotation-hours; spend them either correcting ranked masks or labeling new images with the same tool; train matched models on both results; compare gains.
main_risk: Per-hour rates depend on tooling quality and image difficulty; results need at least two annotation-tool conditions to generalize.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: More training images is the most effective use of annotation budget; existing label noise mostly averages out.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern training may be robust enough to label noise that repair buys little, and diversity from new images may dominate at all sizes.
fastest_falsification: 20-hour pilot per arm on one benchmark subset: one week including training runs.

one_line: Web-scale pretraining corpora are effectively far smaller than advertised: near-duplicate structure makes dense-transfer gains track deduplicated size, not raw size.
problem: Scaling claims quote raw image counts; web corpora contain heavy near-duplicate and template structure, and dense-task transfer may respond only to the deduplicated core.
core_hypothesis: Downstream segmentation transfer correlates with feature-level deduplicated corpus size; adding near-duplicates contributes approximately nothing, so raw-size scaling curves systematically overstate the data lever.
falsifiable_prediction: Pretraining on a deduplicated corpus at 50% raw size will match full-corpus pretraining on segmentation transfer within 0.2 mIoU, while a random 50% subsample (keeping duplicates) falls measurably behind the deduplicated arm at equal raw size.
why_important: Cuts pretraining costs and corrects scaling-law inputs: the honest x-axis is effective (deduplicated) samples; affects both budgeting and scientific conclusions about data scaling.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: deduplication benefits are established for language models; the dense-transfer effective-size accounting for vision corpora appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build three pretraining sets (full, deduped-50, random-50) from one public corpus; pretrain identically; fine-tune segmentation on two benchmarks; compare.
main_risk: Deduplication thresholds are a free parameter; results must be shown across at least two similarity thresholds to avoid threshold-picking accusations.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Raw corpus size is the meaningful data-scaling variable for pretraining vision models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Near-duplicates may act as beneficial natural augmentation for dense features, making raw size the right axis after all.
fastest_falsification: Small-scale version with a modest corpus and one downstream benchmark: about two GPU-weeks.

one_line: Classification-derived dataset-pruning scores pick the wrong images for segmentation; dense-specific pruning keeps quality at much higher pruning rates.
problem: Dataset pruning research shows large fractions of training data are redundant, but the importance scores (forgetting events, gradient norms on class labels) are computed for classification objectives and are being reused for dense tasks unvalidated.
core_hypothesis: Image-level importance for segmentation is driven by boundary configuration diversity, not class-level difficulty; classification scores mis-rank dense value, and a boundary-entropy-based score prunes 2x more aggressively at equal quality.
falsifiable_prediction: At 50% pruning, boundary-diversity scoring will retain within 0.3 mIoU of full-data training while classification-derived scores lose over 1.0 mIoU, on two benchmarks.
why_important: Halving dense training data without loss is directly valuable, and the result would establish that data value is task-structured rather than intrinsic to images.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: dense-specific pruning criteria appear underexplored; most pruning literature validates on classification.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both scoring families on one benchmark, prune at 30/50/70%, train matched models, compare retention curves.
main_risk: Boundary-entropy scoring may correlate strongly with classification difficulty scores in practice, making the comparison a wash rather than a win.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Data-pruning importance scores are task-agnostic: images valuable for classification training are valuable for dense training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation training may be so annotation-cost-dominated that even correct pruning is irrelevant, or classification scores may transfer fine.
fastest_falsification: One pruning rate, both scores, one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Annotation granularity beats image count: fewer images with part-level masks outperform many images with coarse masks at equal annotation time.
problem: Dataset design defaults to maximizing image count at fixed (usually coarse) annotation granularity; the granularity to count exchange rate is unmeasured for modern segmentation training.
core_hypothesis: Detailed annotation (parts, precise boundaries, occlusion order) supervises features that coarse masks over many images never teach; at matched annotation-hours, high-granularity small datasets beat low-granularity large ones on fine-grained downstream tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: A part-annotated dataset consuming the same annotation-hours as a 4x-larger coarse-mask dataset will yield better transfer to boundary-sensitive downstream tasks by over 1 boundary-F point while matching mIoU.
why_important: Dataset construction budgets are enormous; a validated exchange-rate curve between granularity and count would change how the next generation of dense datasets is specified.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: granularity-vs-count tradeoff curves at matched cost appear unpublished for segmentation training.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From one source pool, produce two datasets at equal measured annotation-hours (coarse-many vs fine-few); train identically; evaluate on boundary-sensitive and standard tasks.
main_risk: Annotation-hour measurement is noisy across annotators; requires logging real tool time rather than estimates.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Image diversity (count) is worth more than annotation detail once masks are acceptable quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Diversity may dominate for generalization exactly as believed, with granularity mattering only for niche boundary tasks.
fastest_falsification: Small pilot (200 fine vs 800 coarse at matched hours) with one architecture: one focused week.

one_line: At equal annotation cost, sparse point and scribble supervision matches dense masks, making dense mask labeling economically irrational for many projects.
problem: Weak-supervision papers compare at equal image counts (where dense wins); practitioners budget in annotator-hours, where points and scribbles cover an order of magnitude more images.
core_hypothesis: The marginal information per annotation-second is far higher for sparse labels; at matched wall-clock annotation budgets, point/scribble-supervised modern pipelines land within noise of dense-mask training for most semantic classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Under logged equal annotation-hours, point-supervised training on the resulting larger image set will come within 1 mIoU of dense-mask training on two benchmarks, and will win on classes with simple topology.
why_important: Would reverse the default annotation specification for applied segmentation projects and quantify exactly which classes still require dense masks (complex topology, thin structures).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: cost-normalized comparisons exist in isolated papers with estimated (not logged) costs; a rigorous time-logged comparison with modern pipelines appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a real annotation study logging seconds per image for dense, scribble, and point protocols; train matched pipelines on the equal-budget outputs; stratify results by class topology.
main_risk: Results hinge on the weak-supervision training pipeline quality; a weak pipeline unfairly dooms sparse labels, so the strongest available methods must be used.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Dense masks are the gold-standard training signal worth their cost; weak labels are a compromise for low-budget settings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern architectures may extract disproportionate value from exact boundaries, keeping dense masks ahead even at 10x fewer images.
fastest_falsification: Annotation-time logging on 100 images per protocol plus one training round each: about a week.

one_line: Class-balanced training is not the optimum for segmentation: instance-count balancing beats pixel balancing, and both lose to loss-adaptive sampling.
problem: Balanced sampling is applied to segmentation by pixel frequency out of habit; pixels, instances, and images are different units, and the right balancing unit for dense learning is unresolved.
core_hypothesis: Pixel-frequency balancing overweights large amorphous regions and underweights small-object classes; instance-count balancing aligns better with what limits learning, and simple online loss-proportional sampling beats both static schemes.
falsifiable_prediction: On two long-tail benchmarks, instance-balanced sampling will beat pixel-balanced sampling on tail-class IoU by a clear margin, and loss-adaptive sampling will beat both by over 1 tail-class IoU point at equal compute.
why_important: Balancing choices are silently embedded in every training pipeline; establishing the correct unit is a foundational, immediately reusable result.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: balancing-unit comparisons for dense prediction appear scattered and confounded; a clean three-way controlled study seems missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the three sampling schemes on one long-tail semantic and one instance benchmark, matched compute, 3 seeds, stratified metrics.
main_risk: Loss-adaptive sampling risks instability and feedback loops; divergent runs must be reported, not silently discarded.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Class-balancing by pixel frequency is the appropriate default for imbalanced segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pixel balancing may already approximate the optimum because loss mass tracks pixel mass; the three schemes might converge to similar solutions.
fastest_falsification: Three sampling arms on one benchmark, 2 seeds: several GPU-days.

one_line: Past a modest scale, hard negatives (target-free images) buy more deployed reliability than additional positives, but datasets keep growing positives.
problem: Dataset growth focuses on images containing target classes; deployed segmentation failure is often false positives on target-free scenes (lookalikes, unusual contexts), a data need benchmarks under-serve.
core_hypothesis: The marginal value of a target-free hard-negative image for reducing deployment false positives exceeds that of another positive image once recall saturates; the positives-only growth habit is misallocation.
falsifiable_prediction: At fixed added-image budget, augmenting training with mined hard negatives will reduce false-positive area on target-free test scenes by over 50% while sacrificing under 0.3 recall-side mIoU, beating the same budget of positives on combined deployment metrics.
why_important: Defines a concrete correction to dataset-growth strategy and to benchmark design (target-free test partitions), addressing the metric-invisible half of deployment failure.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: hard-negative mining is standard within training; the dataset-composition-level claim about marginal value of negatives vs positives appears unquantified for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix an added-image budget; compare positive-growth vs mined-negative-growth training arms on a combined metric suite including target-free scenes.
main_risk: Hard-negative mining quality determines the result; a weak miner understates the negatives arm.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Growing the number of annotated positive examples is the main path to better deployed segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pretrained backbones may already suppress lookalike false positives well, leaving little for negatives to fix.
fastest_falsification: One budget, two arms, one deployment-style eval: a few GPU-days plus negative mining.

one_line: Random train/val splits on session-structured datasets leak near-duplicates and inflate segmentation scores; session-stratified splits reorder published methods.
problem: Many segmentation datasets are collected in sessions (same scene, camera, or day); random splitting places near-identical frames on both sides, inflating validation scores and possibly distorting method rankings.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of benchmark performance is same-session memorization; re-splitting by session will drop absolute scores and change method orderings, because methods differ in how much they exploit leakage.
falsifiable_prediction: Session-stratified re-splitting of two commonly used datasets will drop mIoU by several points and flip at least one widely accepted pairwise method ordering trained and evaluated identically on both splits.
why_important: Constructive fix (session-stratified splitting) is trivial to adopt; the finding recalibrates how much published progress is generalization vs leakage. This is a benchmark-hygiene claim with a concrete remedy, not a pure audit.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: near-duplicate leakage is documented for some classification test sets (KNOWN adjacent prior work); a controlled re-split with method-reordering evidence for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cluster images by capture session (metadata or visual near-duplicate detection); create stratified splits; retrain 4 representative methods on both splits; compare scores and orderings.
main_risk: Session inference from visual similarity may over-cluster distinct scenes; metadata-backed datasets should anchor the analysis.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Random splits measure generalization adequately for established segmentation datasets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Leakage may inflate all methods nearly equally, preserving rankings and reducing the finding to a calibration constant.
fastest_falsification: Near-duplicate audit plus re-split evaluation of existing public checkpoints (no retraining) for a first signal: days.

one_line: Verify-and-correct beats from-scratch human annotation on quality, not just cost: the gold-standard hierarchy is backwards.
problem: Model-assisted annotation is accepted for training data but distrusted for evaluation sets on circularity grounds; meanwhile from-scratch human masks carry fatigue and inconsistency errors nobody audits.
core_hypothesis: At equal time budgets, human-verified-and-corrected model masks are closer to careful consensus ground truth than from-scratch human masks, even for evaluation use, because correction focuses human attention where it matters; the circularity concern is manageable with model-diverse proposals.
falsifiable_prediction: Against expensive multi-annotator consensus references, verify-and-correct masks will show lower boundary error than from-scratch masks at matched time, and model-origin bias will be reduced below detectability when proposals come from 3 diverse models.
why_important: If correction pipelines produce better ground truth, evaluation-set construction norms (which currently forbid model assistance) are actively lowering benchmark quality.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: assisted-annotation quality studies exist for speed claims; head-to-head quality-at-matched-time against consensus references with circularity controls appears rare.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build consensus references on 200 images (5 annotators); compare from-scratch vs verify-and-correct single-annotator outputs at matched time; test for residual model-signature bias with model-family holdouts.
main_risk: Model-signature bias may be subtle and only detectable by the held-out model family test; a negative bias test is not proof of absence.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: From-scratch human annotation is the quality gold standard; model-assisted masks are second-class and unsuitable for evaluation sets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anchoring effects may cause correctors to accept plausible-but-wrong model boundaries, producing exactly the contamination the community fears.
fastest_falsification: 200-image dual-protocol study with consensus reference: one to two weeks, annotation-bounded.

one_line: Tail-class segmentation is bottlenecked by head-class boundary quality, not tail sample counts: fixing head labels helps the tail more than adding tail data.
problem: Long-tail remedies focus on getting more tail examples; tail instances are usually embedded next to head-class regions whose noisy boundaries corrupt the tail's effective supervision.
core_hypothesis: A large share of tail-class error is boundary confusion against adjacent head classes; improving head-class boundary label quality (or head-boundary training emphasis) transfers to tail IoU more per unit effort than tail-example collection.
falsifiable_prediction: Correcting only head-class boundaries adjacent to tail instances in training data will improve tail-class IoU by more than adding an equal-effort quantity of new tail examples, on two long-tail benchmarks.
why_important: Counter-intuitive budget guidance for the long-tail problem, and a mechanistic reframing: the tail suffers from its context, not only its scarcity.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: error decompositions attributing tail failure to adjacent-head boundary noise appear absent from the long-tail segmentation literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Decompose tail errors into boundary-adjacent vs interior; run the two intervention arms at matched annotation effort; compare tail IoU gains.
main_risk: The effect may hold only for small-object tail classes with high perimeter-to-area ratios, narrowing applicability.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: The long-tail problem is a sample-scarcity problem solved primarily by acquiring more tail examples.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Tail error may be dominated by classification confusion (wrong class entirely) rather than boundary confusion, in which case head-boundary repair buys little.
fastest_falsification: Error decomposition on existing model predictions for tail classes: two days of analysis before any intervention.

one_line: Strong photometric augmentation narrows models to the benchmark camera pipeline instead of broadening them: on truly novel pipelines it backfires.
problem: Strong augmentation is credited with robustness because it improves scores on benchmark test sets; those test sets share the training set's camera and ISP pipeline, so the evaluation cannot distinguish robustness from pipeline-specific adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Heavy photometric augmentation teaches invariance to the augmentation family, not to real pipeline variation; on images from genuinely different ISPs and sensors, heavily augmented models will lose to lightly augmented ones trained at equal length.
falsifiable_prediction: On cross-ISP test sets (same scenes, different camera processing), models trained with heavy photometric augmentation will underperform light-augmentation models by a measurable margin, reversing their benchmark ordering.
why_important: Deployment robustness advice rests on this belief; if augmentation strength is pipeline-narrowing, the recipe for cross-sensor deployment changes fundamentally (toward raw-domain training or ISP randomization).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: augmentation-vs-real-shift gaps are known in pieces; a controlled cross-ISP reversal test for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or source same-scene multi-ISP imagery (raw reprocessed through multiple pipelines); train augmentation-strength ladder; evaluate cross-pipeline.
main_risk: Multi-ISP paired data is scarce; raw-reprocessing simulation may not capture real ISP diversity, requiring at least one physically distinct camera pair.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Stronger photometric augmentation monotonically improves robustness to real-world imaging variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation families may coincidentally span real ISP variation well, preserving the benefit across pipelines.
fastest_falsification: Reprocess one raw dataset through 3 ISP configurations and evaluate an existing augmentation-ladder of checkpoints: days.

one_line: Copy-paste and CutMix buy region accuracy while corrupting boundary learning: models learn that hard straight edges are class boundaries.
problem: Mixing augmentations improve mIoU and are treated as free; their paste artifacts insert unnatural boundary statistics (hard transitions, no contact shadows) into supervision, potentially teaching wrong boundary priors.
core_hypothesis: Mixing-trained models over-predict crisp artificial-looking boundaries and underperform on soft natural transitions (fur, foliage, shadows); the aggregate mIoU gain hides a boundary-type-conditional loss.
falsifiable_prediction: Mixing-trained models will show improved mIoU but degraded boundary-F specifically on a soft-transition boundary subset, relative to no-mixing controls, across two benchmarks.
why_important: Identifies a hidden cost of a ubiquitous recipe component and motivates artifact-aware mixing (blended composites) with a concrete acceptance test.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: paste-artifact concerns are mentioned qualitatively in copy-paste papers; a boundary-type-stratified cost quantification appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with and without mixing; build a soft-vs-hard boundary partition on test sets; compare stratified boundary metrics; add a blended-mixing arm as the constructive fix.
main_risk: Soft-boundary ground truth is itself noisy, so stratified differences need annotation-noise controls.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Copy-paste style augmentation is a strictly beneficial trick for segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may ignore paste-edge statistics entirely (learning them as augmentation noise), leaving soft-boundary performance untouched.
fastest_falsification: Stratified re-scoring of existing mixing-vs-plain checkpoint pairs: two days if checkpoints exist, else one training pair.

one_line: Multi-scale inference is redundant once crop-scale augmentation is tuned: the machinery survives on under-tuned training baselines.
problem: Multi-scale testing persists as a standard evaluation-time cost; its benefit may be a compensation for inadequate scale coverage during training rather than a genuine inference-time necessity.
core_hypothesis: The gain from multi-scale inference shrinks toward zero as training-time scale augmentation range and sampling are properly tuned; published multi-scale gains are a measure of training-recipe scale-coverage deficiency.
falsifiable_prediction: After tuning crop-scale distribution with a modest search, single-scale inference will come within 0.2 mIoU of multi-scale inference on two benchmarks, versus historical gaps several times larger.
why_important: Eliminates a costly inference-time ritual for deployments and reframes multi-scale gains as a diagnostic of training-recipe deficiency, constructive for recipe design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the interaction between training scale-sampling and inference-time multi-scale benefit appears not systematically mapped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid over training scale ranges; for each, measure single-vs-multi-scale inference gap; show the gap collapsing as coverage improves.
main_risk: Extreme-scale objects (very large or tiny) may always need multi-scale inference, leaving a small irreducible gap that critics can point to.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Multi-scale inference extracts scale information unavailable to any single-scale pass.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale equivariance may be architecturally impossible to train in, keeping the multi-scale gap open regardless of augmentation tuning.
fastest_falsification: Three training scale-ranges, dual-mode evaluation each: several GPU-days.

one_line: Default horizontal flipping measurably harms orientation-dependent classes, and class-averaged metrics hide the damage.
problem: Horizontal flip is applied universally; classes with intrinsic orientation or chirality (text, signage, driving-side conventions, anatomical laterality) receive contradictory supervision under flips, and the harm disappears in class-mean reporting.
core_hypothesis: For an identifiable class subset, flip augmentation reduces per-class IoU relative to no-flip training, while helping the mean; per-class augmentation policies recover both.
falsifiable_prediction: A flip ablation on driving and text-rich benchmarks will show statistically significant per-class degradation on orientation-dependent classes exceeding 1 IoU point, invisible in the class mean.
why_important: Constructively motivates class-conditional augmentation policies (trivial to implement) and warns that the universal-recipe habit costs specific, sometimes safety-relevant classes (signage laterality).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: flip harm is folklore for text recognition; a quantified per-class accounting for segmentation with a policy fix appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train flip/no-flip/class-conditional-flip arms on two benchmarks; report per-class deltas with seed statistics; pre-register the orientation-dependent class list.
main_risk: Orientation-dependent classes are often rare, so per-class deltas need multiple seeds for significance.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Horizontal flipping is a universally safe and beneficial augmentation for natural scenes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may learn orientation-conditional features despite contradictory supervision, showing no measurable per-class harm.
fastest_falsification: Flip-vs-no-flip pair on one benchmark with per-class reporting, 3 seeds: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Color jitter destroys the signal for color-defined classes, and models pass benchmarks anyway by exploiting shape shortcuts that fail in deployment.
problem: Color augmentation is universal, yet some segmentation targets are defined primarily by color (ripeness, corrosion, bruising, inflammation, algae); benchmarks may not expose the loss because their test sets share the shape correlations.
core_hypothesis: Color-jitter-trained models solve color-defined classes via correlated shape/texture shortcuts; under shape-matched color-contrast tests (same object, different condition color), they collapse, while color-jitter-free models retain discrimination.
falsifiable_prediction: On a shape-controlled color-discrimination test built from condition-monitoring imagery, standard-augmentation models will drop by over 50% relative IoU versus their benchmark scores, while no-color-jitter models drop far less.
why_important: Condition-monitoring segmentation (agriculture, industrial inspection, medicine) is exactly where color carries the signal; the universal recipe may be silently crippling these deployments.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: color-shortcut interactions with augmentation are studied for classification texture/shape bias; the dense-prediction condition-class version appears open.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble shape-matched color-varying pairs (same fruit ripe/unripe, same metal rusted/clean); evaluate augmentation-ladder models; report discrimination collapse curves.
main_risk: Building shape-matched pairs at scale is laborious; synthetic recoloring shortcuts would undermine the test's authority.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Color jitter is a safe default that improves robustness without meaningful cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may retain color sensitivity despite jitter (jitter ranges rarely destroy hue ordering), passing the discrimination test fine.
fastest_falsification: 50 shape-matched pairs evaluated on existing checkpoints with and without color-jitter training: days.

one_line: Consistency-regularization training is inference-time ensembling in disguise: its gain equals averaging two augmented predictions of the baseline.
problem: Weak-strong consistency objectives are credited with teaching invariant representations; the measured gain may equal what prediction averaging over augmentations yields at inference, implying no representational improvement.
core_hypothesis: Consistency training distills the baseline's own augmentation-averaged predictions into single-pass form; comparing consistency-trained single-pass models against baseline models evaluated with two-view prediction averaging will show near-identical accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Across two semi-supervised segmentation setups, baseline-plus-two-view-averaging will match consistency-trained single-pass models within 0.3 mIoU, and their per-image errors will be highly correlated.
why_important: Mechanistic clarity about a dominant semi-supervised ingredient: if it is amortized ensembling, the research question becomes how to ensemble better, not how to regularize consistency.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the distillation-of-ensembling interpretation exists theoretically; a direct empirical equivalence test for dense prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train baseline and consistency arms; evaluate baseline with 1-view and 2-view averaged inference; compare accuracy and error correlation against the consistency model.
main_risk: Equivalence in accuracy but divergence in error structure would give a mixed verdict requiring careful interpretation.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Consistency regularization improves the learned representation beyond what inference tricks can achieve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consistency training may show gains on downstream transfer (probing) that inference averaging cannot produce, proving genuine representational change.
fastest_falsification: One consistency setup with the two-view baseline control added: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Augmentation strength should shrink with dataset scale, and past a size threshold strong augmentation becomes net harmful in-domain.
problem: Recipes tuned on small benchmarks (heavy augmentation) are cargo-culted to large proprietary datasets; the augmentation-strength-vs-dataset-size interaction is unmapped for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Augmentation is a bias-variance trade: it adds invariance bias that pays off only when data is scarce; the optimal strength decays with dataset size, crossing to net-harmful for in-domain performance at scales many industrial teams already exceed.
falsifiable_prediction: On nested dataset fractions of a large corpus, the optimal photometric-geometric augmentation strength (by grid search) will decrease monotonically with size, with the strong-augmentation arm losing to light augmentation at the largest scale by a measurable margin.
why_important: Provides a scaling rule for a recipe knob everyone sets by folklore, and warns large-data teams that inherited augmentation defaults may be taxing their models.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: augmentation-size interactions are studied for classification in places; a dense-prediction strength-decay curve appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three dataset scales x four augmentation strengths, matched compute per cell, one benchmark family; map the optimum trajectory.
main_risk: Compute cost of the grid; also OOD robustness may still favor strong augmentation, requiring the claim to stay scoped to in-domain performance.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Strong augmentation recipes transfer across dataset scales; more augmentation rarely hurts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large datasets may still under-cover appearance space enough that augmentation keeps paying, pushing the harm threshold beyond practical scales.
fastest_falsification: Two scales x two strengths (4 cells): a focused GPU-week for the interaction sign.

one_line: Elastic deformation, the canonical medical augmentation, adds nothing on modern architectures: its benefit was a capacity-era artifact.
problem: Elastic deformation is ritually included in medical segmentation pipelines based on early CNN-era evidence; whether it still helps modern high-capacity pretrained models is untested.
core_hypothesis: Elastic deformation helped low-capacity models generalize from tiny datasets by simulating anatomical variation crudely; modern pretrained architectures gain nothing, and unrealistic deformations may even teach false anatomy priors.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating elastic deformation across 4 organ tasks on a modern pretrained pipeline will change Dice by less than seed noise, and on at least one task removal will improve boundary accuracy.
why_important: Medical pipelines accumulate unexamined ritual components; pruning one with a clean null (or discovering task-conditional harm) improves reproducibility and simplifies the recipe space. Flag: medical substrate adjacent to wave-1 worker_B, framed as an augmentation non-replication claim.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: modern ablations of elastic deformation with seed statistics across tasks appear absent; the component is inherited by default in popular frameworks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: With/without elastic deformation on 4 public organ tasks, 5 seeds each, modern pretrained pipeline; report effect sizes with CIs.
main_risk: Popular medical frameworks entangle elastic deformation with other spatial augmentations; a clean ablation needs careful pipeline surgery.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Elastic deformation is an essential, task-agnostic ingredient for medical segmentation performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For very small datasets (a common medical reality) the augmentation may still deliver real gains, keeping the ritual justified where it is used most.
fastest_falsification: Two organ tasks, 3 seeds, with/without arms: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Test-time augmentation increases per-image regressions even while raising the mean: it is not the safe free accuracy it is sold as.
problem: TTA is described as risk-free accuracy; deployment cares about per-image reliability, and averaging over augmented views can flip previously correct predictions on asymmetric or orientation-sensitive content.
core_hypothesis: TTA improves aggregate metrics while increasing the fraction of images that get worse relative to single-pass inference; the regression set is structured (orientation-sensitive scenes, boundary-tight objects), not random noise.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 3 models and 2 benchmarks, TTA will raise mean mIoU while making at least 20% of images worse, and the regressed images will cluster on identifiable content types rather than being metric noise.
why_important: Reliability engineering needs regression-rate accounting, not just means; if TTA redistributes errors, deployment sign-off processes should test it per content type. Constructive: a selective-TTA policy triggered by content classifiers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-image regression analysis of TTA for segmentation appears unreported; papers publish means.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run single-pass and TTA inference for several checkpoints; compute per-image deltas; characterize the regression cluster; test a selective-TTA policy.
main_risk: Regression clusters may be benchmark-idiosyncratic; needs two dissimilar benchmarks to claim structure.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: TTA is a strictly safe way to buy accuracy at inference time.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-image regressions may be tiny in magnitude even if numerous, making the aggregate-vs-reliability tension immaterial in practice.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only per-image delta analysis on existing checkpoints: one day.

one_line: Learned augmentation policies transferred from classification search underperform hand-set simple augmentation for segmentation.
problem: AutoAugment-style policies searched on classification proxies are imported into segmentation pipelines assuming task-transferability of augmentation value.
core_hypothesis: Optimal augmentation for dense prediction differs structurally from classification (geometric fidelity matters, occlusion-simulating cutout interacts with masks); imported learned policies will lose to a simple tuned baseline of crop-flip-jitter under matched tuning budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: On two segmentation benchmarks, classification-searched policies will underperform a 10-trial-tuned simple augmentation baseline by a measurable margin, and dense-searched policies will recover the difference.
why_important: Stops a silent negative transfer in recipe design and motivates (constructively) dense-native augmentation search with mask-aware operations.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: augmentation-policy transferability across task types appears untested for dense prediction specifically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms (imported policy, tuned simple, dense-searched policy) at matched tuning budgets on two benchmarks, 3 seeds.
main_risk: Dense policy search is expensive; the cheap version (imported vs tuned-simple only) answers the negative claim but not the constructive one.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Learned augmentation policies are near-universal recipe upgrades whose value transfers across tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Imported policies may sit close enough to the dense optimum that differences vanish within noise, acquitting the import habit.
fastest_falsification: Imported-vs-tuned-simple pair on one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: The transformers-beat-CNNs verdict for segmentation is a training-recipe artifact, not an architectural fact.
problem: The field migrated to transformer segmenters after comparisons in which architecture, pretraining corpus, recipe, and compute all changed simultaneously; the architecture-specific share of the gap was never isolated for dense tasks.
core_hypothesis: Modern convolutional backbones trained with the identical pretraining data, schedule, augmentation, and decoder as transformer counterparts will match them on standard segmentation benchmarks at equal FLOPs; the residual architectural effect is within noise. VERIFIED PRIOR WORK exists making this argument for classification; the dense-prediction isolation is the open piece.
falsifiable_prediction: A fully recipe-matched CNN-vs-ViT pair at two compute scales will differ by under 0.5 mIoU on ADE20K and Cityscapes, versus multi-point gaps in the original migration-era comparisons.
why_important: Architecture beliefs drive hardware, tooling, and research investment; if the dense-task verdict is a recipe artifact, efficiency-friendly convolutional deployments regain legitimacy.
