why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: classification-side recipe-matching is published; an equally careful segmentation-side study appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched CNN/ViT pairs identically, attach identical decoders, fine-tune identically, 3 seeds, two compute scales.
main_risk: Perfect recipe matching is impossible (some techniques are architecture-specific); the study needs sensitivity analysis over the unavoidable asymmetries.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Transformer architectures are intrinsically better for segmentation than convolutional ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense tasks may specifically reward global attention in ways classification does not, so the gap could survive recipe matching for segmentation even if it vanished for classification.
fastest_falsification: Fine-tune stage only with matched publicly pretrained CNN/ViT pairs where they exist: a GPU-week for a preliminary verdict.

one_line: U-Net skip connections mainly transport boundary detail, not semantics: replacing skip content with edge maps preserves most performance.
problem: Skip connections are explained as fusing multi-level semantics; if their real function is carrying high-frequency spatial alignment, architectural innovation aimed at semantic fusion is optimizing a misunderstanding.
core_hypothesis: Replacing encoder skip features with cheap edge/gradient maps of the input will retain the large majority of segmentation performance, while removing only the semantic content of skips (shuffling channels, projecting to low rank) costs little; the bottleneck path carries semantics alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Edge-map-substituted skips will retain over 90% of baseline Dice/mIoU across 3 U-Net-family tasks, while removing skips entirely costs several points, dissociating alignment value from semantic value.
why_important: Mechanistic understanding redirects decoder design: if skips are alignment channels, explicit cheap alignment signals could replace expensive multi-level fusion machinery.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: skip ablations exist; content-substitution experiments dissociating alignment from semantics appear rare or absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train U-Net variants with (a) normal skips, (b) edge-map skips, (c) semantically-scrambled skips, (d) no skips, on 3 tasks; compare region and boundary metrics.
main_risk: Result may vary with decoder depth and task granularity; needs one natural-image and one medical task at minimum.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Skip connections fuse semantic information across scales, which is why encoder-decoder segmentation works.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For fine-grained multi-class tasks, skip semantics may carry class-discriminative detail that edge maps cannot, breaking the retention prediction.
fastest_falsification: Four skip variants on one task: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Dilated convolutions are a low-resolution-era workaround that modern pipelines no longer need.
problem: Atrous/dilated designs are foundational segmentation lore and still shape architectures, despite originating under GPU-memory constraints that forced low-resolution processing.
core_hypothesis: At modern training resolutions with modern decoders, replacing dilated stages with plain strided stages plus learned upsampling matches accuracy at lower cost; the dilation advantage was contingent on the resolution regime, not fundamental.
falsifiable_prediction: Recipe-matched dilated vs strided variants of the same backbone will differ by under 0.3 mIoU on two benchmarks at current standard resolutions, with the strided variant faster by a clear margin.
why_important: Removes an inherited constraint from architecture search spaces and clarifies which classic design lessons were regime-contingent, a reusable meta-lesson for the field.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: dilation ablations at modern regimes with matched recipes appear not systematically published; the belief persists by inheritance.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train dilated and strided variants of one classic and one modern backbone under identical recipes; compare accuracy-latency frontiers.
main_risk: Some tasks with very large receptive-field needs (scene-level context) may still favor dilation, requiring task-stratified reporting.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Dilated convolutions are an essential ingredient for high-quality semantic segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense per-pixel receptive-field coverage from dilation may still matter at object boundaries, keeping a real gap at matched cost.
fastest_falsification: One backbone pair on one benchmark: days.

one_line: Global attention is wasted on most pixels: windowed attention with zero cross-window communication matches global models on all but a small class subset.
problem: Global context is invoked as the reason attention helps segmentation; the class-conditional structure of that benefit (which pixels actually need long-range evidence) is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: For the large majority of classes, local windows contain sufficient evidence and global attention adds nothing; the global advantage concentrates in a small set of context-defined classes (sky-water disambiguation, scene-dependent surfaces), so global machinery is mostly overhead.
falsifiable_prediction: A communication-ablated windowed model will match a global-attention twin within 0.3 mIoU overall, with the residual gap concentrated in under 15% of classes identifiable a priori as context-defined.
why_important: Yields a class-conditional context taxonomy that guides efficient architecture choice per deployment label set, replacing the vague global-context-is-good narrative with a measured map.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: receptive-field analyses exist; a clean communication-ablation with per-class attribution for modern segmenters appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched global vs strictly-windowed variants; report per-class deltas; test whether a pre-registered context-defined class list predicts where gaps appear.
main_risk: Windowed models may compensate through depth (stacking windows expands effective receptive field), blurring the ablation; needs receptive-field-controlled variants.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Global receptive fields are broadly necessary for strong segmentation performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Long-range dependencies may matter diffusely across many classes in small amounts, producing a spread-out gap that refutes the concentration claim.
fastest_falsification: One matched pair with per-class reporting: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Parameter allocation in segmentation models is backwards: past a modest backbone size, decoder capacity and decoder resolution dominate marginal gains.
problem: Scaling investment goes overwhelmingly into backbones while decoders stay small and low-resolution; the marginal-gain allocation between the two has not been mapped at fixed total budgets.
core_hypothesis: Backbone returns diminish quickly for dense tasks while decoder capacity/resolution returns persist; at fixed total FLOPs, shifting budget from backbone to decoder beats the standard allocation across a wide range.
falsifiable_prediction: On an iso-FLOP grid over backbone-vs-decoder allocation, the empirical optimum will sit at a substantially larger decoder share than any standard configuration uses, winning by over 1 mIoU against backbone-heavy defaults at equal cost.
why_important: A corrected allocation rule is immediately actionable for every practitioner and challenges the backbone-centric scaling culture inherited from classification.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: decoder-scaling studies exist in isolation; an iso-FLOP allocation frontier for segmentation appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix three total FLOP budgets; sweep backbone/decoder allocation at each; train matched recipes; map the frontier.
main_risk: Findings may be decoder-family-specific; two decoder families needed to claim generality.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Backbone scale is where segmentation quality comes from; decoders are lightweight afterthoughts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pretrained-backbone quality may be irreplaceable by decoder capacity (decoders train from scratch), keeping the optimum backbone-heavy.
fastest_falsification: One budget, three allocations: a few GPU-days for the frontier direction.

one_line: Object-query architectures memorize dataset shape priors and lose to per-pixel heads on shape-out-of-distribution instances.
problem: Query-based segmenters win benchmarks, but queries may act as dataset-specific shape templates; benchmark test sets share the training shape distribution, hiding a generalization tax.
core_hypothesis: On instances with unusual poses, truncations, occlusion patterns, or aspect ratios, query-based decoders will underperform recipe-matched per-pixel decoders, reversing the aggregate ordering, because template-like queries fail off-distribution shapes.
falsifiable_prediction: On a shape-OOD test split (constructed by shape-statistic outlier mining from existing datasets), per-pixel heads will beat query heads by a measurable margin despite losing on the standard split.
why_important: Deployment worlds contain shape outliers (accidents, clutter, rare viewpoints) precisely where perception must not fail; a documented architectural fragility would inform safety-critical architecture choice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: query-memorization concerns appear anecdotally; a controlled shape-OOD architecture comparison seems missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Mine shape-outlier instances from existing benchmarks by mask-statistic percentiles; evaluate matched query vs per-pixel models; compare stratified instance-level metrics.
main_risk: Shape outliers correlate with annotation errors; the outlier split needs manual verification to be credible.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Query-based mask decoders are strictly stronger than per-pixel heads for instance-aware segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Queries may be content-adaptive rather than template-like, generalizing to odd shapes as well as per-pixel heads do.
fastest_falsification: Outlier mining plus evaluation of existing public checkpoints of both families: days, no training.

one_line: Positional embeddings let segmenters memorize benchmark layout statistics; part of reported progress is layout memorization, not perception.
problem: Driving and indoor benchmarks have strong spatial regularities (road below, sky above); models with positional embeddings can exploit them, and test sets with the same layout statistics reward it as if it were perception.
core_hypothesis: A measurable fraction of benchmark mIoU comes from position-conditional priors rather than appearance evidence; on layout-shuffled or layout-atypical imagery, position-equipped models degrade more than position-ablated ones, and method rankings compress.
falsifiable_prediction: Position-ablated models will lose under 1 mIoU on layout-regular benchmarks but outperform position-equipped twins on layout-atypical test imagery (rotated cameras, unusual viewpoints) by a larger margin.
why_important: Distinguishes perception progress from layout priors in reported numbers and warns that viewpoint changes in deployment (different camera mounting) silently break position-dependent models. Constructive: position-robust evaluation imagery as a standard artifact.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: positional-shortcut analyses exist for classification and detection in places; a layout-memorization quantification for segmentation benchmarks appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train position-equipped and position-ablated twins; evaluate on standard, camera-rotated, and viewpoint-shifted test imagery; decompose the gaps.
main_risk: Position ablation can harm optimization independently of priors; needs relative-position controls to separate optimization from memorization effects.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Positional information in segmentation models encodes benign geometric structure, not benchmark-specific shortcuts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Layout priors may be legitimate deployable knowledge (cameras are mounted consistently), making memorization the right behavior rather than a flaw.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate existing models on camera-rotated versions of a benchmark: one day.

one_line: Full-resolution inference is mostly wasted compute: half-resolution prediction with a learned edge-aware upsampler matches it.
problem: Inference cost scales quadratically with resolution, and the community assumes native-resolution processing is required for quality; the actual information content of the extra resolution for segmentation decisions is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation-relevant evidence saturates below native resolution for most content; a cheap guided upsampler consuming the low-resolution prediction plus the full-resolution image recovers boundary precision, matching full-resolution inference at a fraction of cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Half-resolution inference plus guided upsampling will come within 0.3 mIoU and 1 boundary-F point of full-resolution inference on two benchmarks, at under 40% of the FLOPs.
why_important: If the resolution belief is wrong, deployment efficiency doubles for free across the industry; if it is right, the experiment quantifies exactly which content needs native resolution (thin structures), guiding adaptive-resolution designs.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: guided upsampling modules exist; the contrarian claim that they make native-resolution inference redundant as a default appears untested as a general statement.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate resolution ladders with and without guided upsampling across content strata (thin structures, texture boundaries) on two benchmarks.
main_risk: Thin-structure classes (poles, wires) may genuinely need native resolution, making the claim class-conditional rather than general.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Native-resolution inference is necessary for high-quality segmentation, especially boundaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary precision may be exactly where low-resolution evidence is insufficient in ways guided upsampling cannot repair, preserving the full-resolution requirement.
fastest_falsification: Train one guided upsampler on one benchmark and run the ladder comparison: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Normalization-statistic choices move segmentation results more than the architectural contributions claimed in the same papers.
problem: Cross-paper comparisons treat normalization configuration (sync-BN vs frozen-BN vs GN, batch size interactions) as implementation detail, while it may be a dominant hidden variable behind reported architecture gains.
core_hypothesis: Re-running representative method pairs under standardized normalization settings will shrink or flip a substantial fraction of published architectural gaps; normalization variance exceeds median claimed method deltas in the segmentation literature.
falsifiable_prediction: For 6 published-style method pairs, the spread of results across 3 normalization configurations will exceed the originally claimed method gap in at least half the pairs.
why_important: Establishes normalization reporting and standardization as a review requirement, converting a folklore suspicion into measured policy; constructive deliverable is a normalization-sensitivity protocol.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: normalization sensitivity is known qualitatively; its magnitude relative to claimed method effects in segmentation appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six method pairs x three normalization configs x 3 seeds on one benchmark; compare within-pair normalization spread to claimed gaps.
main_risk: Expensive matrix; can be reduced by selecting pairs with public code and small models.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Published architecture-vs-architecture segmentation gaps reflect design quality, with normalization as neutral plumbing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern recipes may have converged on normalization settings enough that the spread is small, acquitting cross-paper comparisons.
fastest_falsification: Two pairs x three configs: a GPU-week for the headline ratio.

one_line: Feature-pyramid fusion is redundant with modern pretrained backbones: the right single scale matches multi-scale fusion.
problem: FPN-style multi-level fusion is default segmentation plumbing inherited from weak-backbone eras; strong pretrained features may already carry multi-scale information within single levels.
core_hypothesis: For modern large pretrained backbones, a single well-chosen feature level with a competent decoder matches full pyramid fusion within noise; fusion machinery survives by inertia and weak ablation practice.
falsifiable_prediction: Single-level variants (best level selected on validation) will come within 0.3 mIoU of full-FPN twins on two benchmarks with large pretrained backbones, while the gap remains large for small from-scratch backbones.
why_important: Simplifies architectures and clarifies that component value is backbone-regime-dependent; the interaction (fusion value vs backbone strength) is the reusable scientific content.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: single-level decoders have precedents for plain ViTs; the general regime-interaction claim (fusion value collapses with backbone strength) appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross backbone strength (small scratch, medium, large pretrained) with decoder input (single level vs pyramid); map the interaction surface.
main_risk: Small-object classes may retain a real pyramid advantage at all regimes, making the claim class-conditional.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Multi-scale feature fusion is necessary infrastructure for accurate segmentation across object sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pyramid fusion may remain decisively better on small objects everywhere, in which case the redundancy claim fails except on object-size-homogeneous tasks.
fastest_falsification: Large-backbone single-level vs pyramid pair on one benchmark: days.

one_line: Temporal-consistency losses buy smoothness, not accuracy: they trade boundary fidelity for reduced flicker and the trade is hidden by reporting choices.
problem: Video segmentation papers add temporal-consistency objectives and report both accuracy and stability improvements; the two may actually be in tension, with accuracy numbers propped up by other recipe changes.
core_hypothesis: Consistency losses low-pass the prediction sequence: flicker metrics improve, but per-frame boundary accuracy on moving objects degrades because the model smooths across genuine motion; controlled ablations will show the tension.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding a standard temporal-consistency loss to a fixed per-frame pipeline will improve temporal-stability metrics while reducing boundary-F on fast-moving objects by a measurable margin, with overall mIoU roughly flat, across two video benchmarks.
why_important: Deployment teams tune for the metric that matters to them; documenting the smoothness-accuracy trade prevents accidentally shipping laggy masks for fast motion (AR, robotics) under the banner of stability.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the trade is plausible from first principles; a motion-stratified accounting of consistency losses appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One per-frame baseline plus consistency-loss variant, evaluated with motion-stratified boundary metrics and flicker metrics on two video segmentation benchmarks.
main_risk: Motion stratification requires flow estimates whose errors correlate with exactly the fast-motion strata of interest; needs synthetic-video controls with exact motion.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Temporal-consistency regularization improves video segmentation quality overall.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Consistency may act mostly on static regions (where smoothing is free), leaving moving boundaries untouched and refuting the tension claim.
fastest_falsification: One loss ablation with motion-stratified metrics on one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Memory-based video object segmentation anti-scales with memory length on long videos: more stored frames means more drift, not more accuracy.
problem: Memory architectures assume that retaining more past frames monotonically helps; on long videos, stored errors compound as they are matched against, and the memory-length-vs-quality curve is unmapped beyond short benchmark clips.
core_hypothesis: Past an optimal horizon, additional memory frames contaminated with earlier prediction errors increase drift; quality versus memory length is non-monotonic, and the optimum shrinks as video length grows.
falsifiable_prediction: On long-video evaluations, sweeping memory capacity will show an interior optimum, with the largest memory configuration losing measurably to a mid-sized one, reversing the short-clip ordering.
why_important: Long-form video (surveillance, surgery recordings, wildlife monitoring) is where these systems deploy; an anti-scaling law for memory changes architecture and eviction-policy priorities constructively.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: drift is a known qualitative failure; a quantified memory-length anti-scaling curve with video-length interaction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a public memory-based VOS model across memory-size settings on short vs long video suites; plot quality against memory length per duration bucket.
main_risk: Long-video ground truth is scarce; may require sparse-frame annotation or synthetic long sequences with exact masks.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Bigger memory banks monotonically improve memory-based video segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Confidence-gated memory writing in modern systems may already suppress drift, keeping the curve monotonic in practice.
fastest_falsification: Memory-size sweep on existing checkpoints over available long clips: days, inference only.

one_line: Optical-flow label propagation now produces worse training signal than per-frame pseudo-labeling: modern model quality has crossed the flow-error floor.
problem: Propagating sparse annotations through video via optical flow is standard for cheap dense supervision; flow errors set a noise floor that used to be below model error but may no longer be.
core_hypothesis: Per-frame pseudo-labels from a strong modern image segmenter now exceed flow-propagated label quality except over very short temporal gaps; pipelines built on propagation are training on noisier labels than the free alternative.
falsifiable_prediction: Training a student on flow-propagated labels versus per-frame teacher pseudo-labels (matched label counts) will favor the pseudo-label arm by a clear margin on two video datasets, with propagation winning only within 2-3 frames of the annotated frame.
why_important: Redirects annotation-economics for video: sparse-frame human labels plus per-frame teachers may dominate the propagation machinery an entire tooling ecosystem is built around.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: the crossover claim (teacher quality vs flow-noise floor) appears untested; both pipelines are used side by side without direct comparison.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a sparse annotation budget; produce dense labels via both pipelines; train identical students; evaluate on held-out human-labeled frames; stratify by temporal distance from annotations.
main_risk: The verdict depends on domain motion statistics; slow-motion domains may keep propagation competitive, requiring at least two motion regimes.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Flow-based propagation is the efficient way to densify sparse video annotations for training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Propagated labels preserve instance identity through time in ways per-frame teachers cannot, which may matter more than boundary noise for video tasks.
fastest_falsification: Label-quality audit (both pipelines against held-out human frames) before any training: two days.

one_line: Semi-supervised VOS leaderboards reward template matching, not segmentation: rankings invert when initialization is category-level instead of first-frame masks.
problem: The dominant VOS protocol provides a perfect first-frame mask, making the task substantially appearance-template tracking; deployed systems rarely receive perfect first-frame masks, and model rankings may not survive protocol changes.
core_hypothesis: Architectures optimized for first-frame-mask protocols overfit to template matching; under noisy-mask, box, or text initialization, the ranking of top methods changes substantially, revealing protocol-specific rather than general video segmentation ability.
falsifiable_prediction: Across the top methods on a standard VOS benchmark, rank correlation between first-frame-mask performance and degraded-initialization performance will fall below 0.5, with at least two ranking inversions among the top five.
why_important: If leaderboard order is protocol-bound, method selection for real systems is being made on the wrong signal; the constructive deliverable is a protocol-battery evaluation standard.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: initialization-robustness of VOS models is occasionally probed; a systematic rank-stability study across initialization protocols appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 6 public VOS models under four initialization protocols (perfect mask, dilated noisy mask, box, none/category); compute rank correlations across protocols.
main_risk: Some protocols require adapters (box-to-mask conversion) whose quality varies per method, needing a shared adapter to keep comparisons fair.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: VOS benchmark rankings reflect general video segmentation ability transferable to deployment settings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong methods may be strong for fundamental reasons (feature quality) that survive protocol changes, keeping rank correlation high.
fastest_falsification: Four-protocol evaluation of public checkpoints: days, inference only.

one_line: Video segmenters exploit benchmark frame-rate statistics: performance collapses off-rate, and trivial frame duplication recovers it, exposing sampling shortcuts.
problem: Models are trained and evaluated at benchmark frame rates; deployment cameras run at different and variable rates, and the community assumes graceful degradation across rates.
core_hypothesis: Temporal modules tune to the specific inter-frame displacement statistics of training frame rates; performance at halved or doubled rates drops non-linearly, and naive tricks (duplicating or dropping frames to restore training-like displacement statistics) recover most of the loss, proving the models exploit sampling statistics rather than motion dynamics.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating video segmenters at 2x and 0.5x native frame rates will show disproportionate degradation, and displacement-normalizing frame manipulation will recover over 70% of the lost accuracy without retraining.
why_important: Frame-rate brittleness matters for every real camera pipeline; the recovery-by-duplication result would show cheaply that the failure is statistical shortcutting, guiding rate-robust training design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: frame-rate sensitivity is occasionally noted; the shortcut diagnosis via displacement-normalization recovery appears new as a designed experiment.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 3 public video models across resampled frame rates with and without displacement-normalizing manipulations; plot degradation and recovery curves.
main_risk: Resampling artifacts (motion blur mismatch at synthetic rates) could contaminate the measurement; needs natively multi-rate captures for the clean version.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Video segmentation models learn motion dynamics that generalize across reasonable frame-rate variation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models with explicit motion estimation may normalize displacements internally, degrading gracefully and refuting the shortcut account.
fastest_falsification: Rate-resampled evaluation of public checkpoints: two days, inference only.

one_line: Offline video segmentation rankings invert under latency-aware streaming evaluation: the accuracy leaderboard is selecting the wrong models for deployment.
problem: Video segmentation is ranked by offline accuracy where compute time is free; deployed systems pay for latency with stale predictions on moved scenes, and heavy accurate models may lose end-to-end. VERIFIED PRIOR WORK exists formalizing streaming evaluation for detection; segmentation-side consequences remain under-adopted.
core_hypothesis: Under streaming evaluation that charges each model its own latency against moving scenes, mid-sized models will beat the offline leaders, and the offline-to-streaming rank correlation will be low enough to invalidate offline rankings as deployment guidance.
falsifiable_prediction: Streaming re-evaluation of 8 public video/image segmenters on driving footage will produce at least three top-five rank inversions relative to offline mIoU ordering at realistic hardware settings.
why_important: If the community optimizes a metric anti-correlated with deployed utility in the relevant regime, model development effort is partially misdirected; a segmentation streaming benchmark is the constructive product.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified for segmentation specifics: the streaming concept is established for detection (VERIFIED PRIOR WORK); the segmentation ranking-inversion magnitude and its dependence on mask granularity are the open questions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement latency-charged streaming scoring for segmentation on an existing annotated video set; evaluate a model zoo spanning sizes; compare orderings.
main_risk: Results are hardware-relative; must report across two or three compute tiers to avoid single-platform conclusions.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Higher offline segmentation accuracy translates to better deployed video perception.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With modern accelerators the latency spread across model sizes may be too small to flip rankings, preserving offline ordering.
fastest_falsification: Latency profiling plus streaming-scored replay of existing predictions: under a week.

one_line: Dedicated video architectures lose to temporally-ensembled per-frame models at matched compute on stable-camera domains.
problem: The field assumes temporal architectures are necessary for video segmentation; for the large deployed class of fixed or stabilized cameras, cheap temporal aggregation of per-frame outputs may match them at equal compute.
core_hypothesis: The value of learned temporal modeling concentrates in egomotion-heavy content; on stable-camera video, per-frame models with output-space temporal smoothing match dedicated video architectures, making the architectural investment regime-specific.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched FLOPs per output frame, per-frame-plus-smoothing will come within 0.5 mIoU of dedicated video models on stable-camera datasets while losing clearly on egomotion-heavy driving footage.
why_important: Gives deployment engineers a validated decision rule (camera motion regime determines architecture class) and deflates the universal claim that video needs temporal architectures.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-frame-vs-video comparisons exist but rarely matched for compute and stratified by camera-motion regime.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare matched-compute pairs on one stable-camera suite (surveillance-style) and one egomotion suite (driving); report the regime interaction.
main_risk: Output-space smoothing choice matters; a weak smoother strawmans the per-frame arm, so two smoothing methods should be included.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Learned temporal modeling is broadly necessary for high-quality video segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even stable scenes contain object motion and occlusion dynamics that learned temporal features may handle far better than output smoothing.
fastest_falsification: One matched-compute pair per regime using public models: days, mostly inference.

one_line: Mask-propagation annotation tools save far less human time than claimed: verification of propagated masks costs nearly as much as drawing for deformable objects.
problem: Annotation-tool papers advertise large savings from propagating masks across frames; claimed savings count drawing time but often ignore the verification burden, which for deformable or fast-moving objects approaches drawing cost.
core_hypothesis: End-to-end annotation time (propagate, inspect, correct) for deformable-object video approaches from-scratch time because humans must scrutinize every propagated boundary; savings are real only for rigid slow objects, a fraction of real content.
falsifiable_prediction: A time-logged annotation study will show under 25% net time savings for deformable categories (people, animals) versus over 60% for rigid static objects, with published-style savings estimates reproduced only when verification time is excluded.
why_important: Annotation budgets for video datasets are planned on these savings claims; correcting the accounting changes tool design priorities toward verification-efficiency rather than propagation quality alone.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: tool papers self-report savings; independent time-logged accounting stratified by object rigidity appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a controlled annotation study (3 annotators, logged tool time, rigidity-stratified content) comparing propagate-and-correct versus from-scratch protocols to consistent quality thresholds.
main_risk: Annotator skill variance is large; needs within-annotator crossover design to control it.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Propagation-based video annotation tools cut labeling cost dramatically across content types.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern propagation quality may be high enough that spot-check verification suffices, keeping savings large even for deformable content.
fastest_falsification: Small crossover study (2 annotators, 20 clips): under a week including analysis.

one_line: Self-training gains anti-correlate with baseline strength and extrapolate to zero exactly where practitioners want to use them.
problem: Pseudo-label self-training is recommended broadly; published gains cluster in weak-baseline regimes (few labels, dated backbones), and the gain-vs-baseline-quality relationship is never plotted.
core_hypothesis: Self-training corrects errors the model can already almost fix; its gain decays roughly linearly with baseline quality, reaching zero (or negative, via confirmation bias) at the strong-baseline operating points of modern pretrained pipelines.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a baseline-quality ladder (varying labels and pretraining), plotting self-training gain versus baseline mIoU will show monotonic decay, with gains statistically indistinguishable from zero at the strongest two rungs.
why_important: Practitioners with strong pipelines may be spending large compute on a technique that cannot help them; the decay curve gives an actionable applicability threshold.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: individual strong-baseline null results likely exist unpublished; the systematic gain-decay curve for segmentation self-training appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Six-rung baseline ladder on one benchmark; identical self-training protocol per rung; plot gain versus baseline with seed error bars.
main_risk: Self-training hyperparameters may need per-rung retuning; frozen hyperparameters would bias against high rungs, so each rung needs a small tuning budget.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Self-training with pseudo-labels is a general-purpose improvement applicable at any baseline strength.
why_it_might_be_wrong: On unlabeled data much more diverse than the labeled pool, self-training may keep helping even strong baselines, breaking the decay-to-zero prediction.
fastest_falsification: Three-rung ladder version: a GPU-week for the trend.

one_line: Semi-supervised segmentation gains evaporate when the unlabeled pool is distribution-shifted from the labeled pool, which is the realistic case.
problem: Benchmarks draw labeled and unlabeled data from the same distribution; real unlabeled pools (fleet data, web scrapes) are shifted, and method rankings and gains under shift are unknown.
core_hypothesis: Consistency and pseudo-label methods rely on the unlabeled distribution matching the test distribution; under realistic shift, most methods lose their gains and several drop below the labeled-only baseline via error amplification on shifted content.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-running 5 representative semi-supervised methods with shifted unlabeled pools (different city, weather, sensor) will reduce median gain by over 70%, with at least one method going negative versus labeled-only.
why_important: The realistic-deployment version of the benchmark is the one practitioners face; documenting the gap redirects research toward shift-robust semi-supervision and honest benchmark design.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: shifted-unlabeled-pool evaluations exist sporadically; a systematic multi-method segmentation study appears missing. Flag: adjacent to wave-2 worker_A domain-shift territory; framed here as a non-replication stress test of semi-supervised claims.
minimal_falsification_experiment: One labeled source; matched and shifted unlabeled pools of equal size; 5 methods; compare gains across pool conditions.
main_risk: Shift magnitude is a free variable; needs a small ladder of shift strengths to characterize the decay rather than one arbitrary point.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Semi-supervised segmentation methods deliver their benchmark gains on whatever unlabeled data is available.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some methods may exploit shifted pools as free domain randomization, retaining or even increasing gains under mild shift.
fastest_falsification: One method, matched-vs-shifted pools: a few GPU-days.

one_line: A decade of CAM-based weakly-supervised segmentation progress compresses to near-noise under a unified fair-tuning protocol.
problem: Weakly-supervised segmentation methods build on class-activation-map seeds with many hand-set thresholds and priors; each paper tunes its own stack, and cross-paper deltas may reflect tuning asymmetry rather than method content.
core_hypothesis: Under a unified protocol that cross-validates thresholds, saliency priors, and post-processing for every method with equal budgets, the spread among a decade of representative methods shrinks to a small fraction of the claimed cumulative progress.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-implementing 8 representative methods under equal-budget unified tuning will compress their range by at least half, and the chronological ordering will no longer be monotonic.
why_important: Establishes how much of a subfield's apparent progress is real, and delivers a constructive shared evaluation harness that future weak-supervision work can adopt; guards against tuning-artifact literatures forming elsewhere.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: fair-benchmark re-implementations exist in other subfields; weakly-supervised segmentation lacks one to my knowledge (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Unified codebase, 8 methods, equal tuning budgets, 3 seeds, two benchmarks; publish the compressed-vs-claimed progress comparison.
main_risk: Reimplementation fidelity disputes are certain; releasing all code and per-method correspondence with original numbers is mandatory.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Weakly-supervised segmentation has made steady method-driven progress over the past decade.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A subset of methods may hold real gains under fair tuning, converting the result from a debunking to a ranking correction.
fastest_falsification: Three methods spanning the decade under the unified protocol: a GPU-week for the compression trend.

one_line: Confidence-thresholded pseudo-labeling silently deletes rare classes: aggregate gains coexist with tail-class collapse below the labeled-only baseline.
problem: Pseudo-label pipelines keep only high-confidence predictions; confidence correlates with class frequency, so tail classes are systematically excluded from the pseudo-supervision the method feeds on.
core_hypothesis: Iterative confidence-filtered self-training amplifies class priors: tail-class recall in pseudo-labels shrinks each round, and final tail-class IoU lands below the labeled-only baseline even as mIoU rises, a harm invisible in headline numbers.
falsifiable_prediction: On long-tail benchmarks, standard self-training will improve mean mIoU while reducing the bottom-decile class IoU relative to labeled-only training, and pseudo-label class distributions will show measurable tail erosion per round.
why_important: Semi-supervised methods are deployed in safety- and equity-sensitive settings where tail classes matter most; a documented tail-erosion mechanism with a measurement protocol prevents silent harm. Constructive fix to test: prior-corrected thresholds.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: class-imbalance interactions with pseudo-labeling are known qualitatively for classification; round-by-round tail-erosion accounting for segmentation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a standard self-training loop with per-round pseudo-label class statistics and per-class test metrics on two long-tail benchmarks; add prior-corrected-threshold arm.
main_risk: Tail-class metrics are high variance; needs multiple seeds and possibly merged tail buckets for statistical power.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Self-training gains are broadly distributed across classes; confidence filtering is a neutral quality control.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-balanced sampling inside modern recipes may counteract erosion, keeping tail classes flat rather than collapsing.
fastest_falsification: Instrumented two-round self-training on one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Unlabeled data anti-scales in semi-supervised segmentation: beyond a labeled-to-unlabeled ratio, more unlabeled data hurts.
problem: The community assumes more unlabeled data monotonically helps semi-supervised learning; with a fixed labeled anchor, growing unlabeled pools may increase pseudo-label error mass faster than signal.
core_hypothesis: Pseudo-label quality control degrades as the unlabeled pool grows relative to labeled anchors (more content outside the labeled support), so performance versus unlabeled-pool size is non-monotonic with an interior optimum tied to the labeled set's coverage.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping unlabeled pool size at fixed labeled size will show performance peaking at an intermediate ratio and declining at the largest pools, on at least two method families; the optimum will shift right as labeled diversity increases.
why_important: An anti-scaling law for unlabeled data would change data-collection strategy (curate unlabeled pools to labeled support) and challenge the more-data-is-safe assumption embedded in semi-supervised practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: unlabeled-scale ablations in papers rarely extend past small ratios; the non-monotonicity claim for segmentation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed labeled set; unlabeled pools at 5 sizes spanning two orders of magnitude; two methods; 3 seeds; locate the optimum and its labeled-diversity dependence.
main_risk: Very large unlabeled pools raise compute costs; the decline may also be method-version-specific, requiring modern strong recipes to be included.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: More unlabeled data is at worst neutral and generally beneficial for semi-supervised segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong filtering heuristics in modern methods may make extra unlabeled data harmless, keeping the curve flat rather than declining.
fastest_falsification: Three pool sizes with one method: a few GPU-days for the curve shape.

one_line: Active learning for segmentation stops beating random sampling once modern pretrained initializations are used.
problem: Active-learning papers demonstrate gains from clever acquisition functions, mostly with weak initializations and tiny seed sets; modern practice starts from strong pretrained models where the informativeness landscape is different.
core_hypothesis: Strong pretraining flattens the acquisition landscape: uncertainty- and diversity-based selection choose images whose marginal value no longer exceeds random selection, so published AL gains fail to replicate in the regime practitioners actually occupy.
falsifiable_prediction: With modern pretrained backbones and realistic batch sizes, 4 representative acquisition functions will beat random by under 0.3 mIoU per round on two benchmarks, versus multi-point historical claims.
why_important: Annotation-planning teams pay real complexity costs for AL machinery; a regime-conditioned null result would simplify pipelines and refocus research on acquisition for genuinely novel content.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: AL-skepticism results exist for classification; a pretrained-regime replication for dense prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: AL simulation with modern initialization, 5 rounds, realistic batch sizes, 4 acquisition functions plus random, two benchmarks, 3 seeds.
main_risk: AL simulations depend on labeling-cost models; per-image versus per-region costing could change conclusions and both should be reported.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Active learning meaningfully reduces annotation cost for segmentation over random sampling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In long-tail or shifted-pool settings acquisition functions may retain large gains, confining the null to iid benchmark conditions.
fastest_falsification: Two acquisition functions vs random, three rounds, one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Retraining on human-corrected model outputs plateaus early: correction data inherits the model's boundary style and cannot teach past it.
problem: Production pipelines retrain on masks produced by annotators correcting model predictions; anchoring means corrected masks stay near model outputs, potentially feeding the model its own style back.
core_hypothesis: Correction-derived labels are biased toward the correcting model's boundary conventions and error blind spots; successive retraining rounds converge to a self-confirming fixed point below the quality achievable with from-scratch labels of equal count.
falsifiable_prediction: Two retraining generations on correction-derived labels will show shrinking gains and a final quality measurably below a from-scratch-label control at matched label counts, with corrected-mask-to-model-output agreement exceeding independent-annotation agreement baselines.
why_important: Correction loops are the default industrial data flywheel; a documented fixed-point pathology with an agreement-based early-warning metric would protect long-run data quality investments.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: annotation anchoring is documented in HCI contexts; its multi-generation training consequence for segmentation appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run two data flywheel generations (correct, retrain, correct) versus a from-scratch labeling control at matched budgets; track agreement statistics and test quality per generation.
main_risk: Effect size depends on annotator diligence incentives; requires realistic (not laboratory-motivated) annotation conditions to be externally valid.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Human-corrected model outputs are equivalent to fresh labels for continued training, at lower cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anchoring may be small for conscientious annotators with good tools, making correction data effectively fresh and the flywheel sound.
fastest_falsification: Single-generation agreement audit (corrected masks vs model outputs vs independent annotations on the same images): days, annotation-bounded.

one_line: Point-supervision parity claims hide a class-structure asymmetry: parity holds for compact things, fails badly for stuff and perforated objects.
problem: Papers report point- or scribble-supervised training approaching full-mask performance in aggregate; the class-conditional structure of the remaining gap is unexamined, so the applicability boundary of cheap supervision is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Sparse supervision suffices where region extent is inferable from local appearance (compact things) and fails where extent is topology-driven (stuff boundaries, perforated and thin structures); the aggregate parity is a class-mix artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: Class-stratified analysis will show sparse-supervised models within 2 IoU of full-mask models on compact thing classes but more than 8 IoU behind on perforated/thin/stuff classes, consistently across two benchmarks.
why_important: Turns a vague parity claim into an actionable supervision-routing rule (which classes need dense masks), directly usable for annotation budget design; also explains conflicting results across datasets as class-mix differences.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: aggregate comparisons abound; a topology-stratified decomposition of the sparse-vs-dense gap appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train sparse- and dense-supervised twins on two benchmarks; group classes by compactness/topology statistics computed from GT; test the interaction.
main_risk: Class topology statistics correlate with class frequency, requiring frequency-controlled comparisons to isolate the topology effect.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Point and scribble supervision get close enough to full masks to be general-purpose replacements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pairwise-affinity losses may already solve extent inference for stuff classes, closing the stratified gap and validating the parity claim broadly.
fastest_falsification: Stratified re-analysis of any published sparse-vs-dense checkpoint pair: two days if checkpoints exist.

one_line: Semi-supervised segmentation results are contaminated by unlabeled-pool overlap with test distributions: dedup shrinks reported gains.
problem: Unlabeled pools are often drawn from the same underlying capture campaigns as test sets; models effectively train (via pseudo-labels) on near-duplicates of test content, inflating semi-supervised gains.
core_hypothesis: A measurable share of published-style semi-supervised gains comes from unlabeled-test near-duplicate leakage; feature-level deduplication between unlabeled pools and test sets will reduce gains, most strongly for memorization-prone methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Deduplicating unlabeled pools against test sets (visual similarity threshold swept) will reduce semi-supervised gains by over 30% relative on at least one standard benchmark configuration, with the reduction growing as the similarity threshold loosens.
why_important: Benchmark hygiene: if gains partly measure leakage, method comparisons are distorted; the dedup protocol is a cheap constructive standard for future semi-supervised evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: leakage audits exist for supervised test sets; the unlabeled-pool-to-test channel in semi-supervised segmentation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute near-duplicate structure between standard unlabeled pools and test sets; re-run two methods with deduplicated pools; compare gain deltas across similarity thresholds.
main_risk: Legitimate distributional closeness versus near-duplication is a continuum; conclusions must be presented across thresholds, not at one cherry-picked point.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Semi-supervised gains measured on standard splits reflect generalization, not unlabeled-test leakage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deduplication may leave gains intact, certifying the benchmarks and reducing this to a due-diligence result.
fastest_falsification: Near-duplicate audit between pools and test sets (no retraining): two days for the exposure estimate.

one_line: Foundation-model masks as free supervision cap student quality below human-label training: teacher biases are inherited, not averaged out.
problem: Pipelines increasingly replace human annotation with promptable-foundation-model masks at scale, assuming volume compensates for per-mask quality deficits.
core_hypothesis: Foundation teachers make systematic (not random) errors: over-crisp boundaries on soft transitions, part-whole inconsistency, and class-conditional blind spots; students inherit these biases, so scaling teacher-labeled data converges to the teacher's error manifold rather than to human-level quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Students trained on 10x teacher-generated masks will remain measurably below students trained on 1x human masks on boundary-type-stratified metrics, and student error maps will correlate with teacher error maps far above chance.
why_important: The annotation-free training narrative underpins current dataset economics; quantifying the inherited-bias ceiling tells the field what foundation supervision can and cannot replace, and motivates bias-breaking hybrid labeling.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: distillation bias inheritance is known in principle; a scaling-versus-bias-ceiling study for promptable-teacher segmentation supervision appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train students on teacher-mask datasets at 1x/3x/10x scale versus a human-mask control; measure quality plateau and teacher-student error correlation.
main_risk: Teacher quality varies with prompting strategy; the study must fix a defensible strong prompting protocol or sweep it.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Scaling foundation-model-generated masks substitutes for human annotation in training segmentation models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Teacher errors may be diverse enough across prompts and images to act like noise, letting scale average them out and refuting the ceiling.
fastest_falsification: 1x-vs-10x teacher-mask student pair plus error-correlation analysis: about a GPU-week.

one_line: A sizeable share of recent benchmark deltas sit below the ground-truth reproducibility floor, making them unfalsifiable as scientific claims.
problem: Method papers claim superiority via sub-point mIoU deltas; the reproducibility noise of the ground truth itself (re-annotation variance) defines a floor below which deltas cannot be attributed to model quality, and that floor is unpublished for major benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: Re-annotation experiments will show benchmark-specific noise floors large enough that a substantial fraction of recent claimed improvements fall below them; the community is publishing differences that the measurement instrument cannot resolve.
falsifiable_prediction: Dual independent re-annotation of 300-image subsets on two major benchmarks will yield mIoU-equivalent noise floors above 0.5 points, exceeding a nontrivial share of recent leaderboard deltas on those benchmarks.
why_important: Constructive deliverable: published noise floors per benchmark plus a reporting norm (claims below floor flagged as unresolved). This raises the evidentiary bar without new infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: inter-annotator variability is studied for specific datasets; benchmark-level noise floors framed against leaderboard delta distributions appear unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Commission dual-protocol re-annotations of benchmark subsets; compute score variation of fixed model outputs across annotation versions; compare against distributions of published deltas.
main_risk: Annotation vendor quality shapes the floor estimate; needs two independent annotation teams for credibility.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Reported mIoU differences on standard benchmarks, however small, reflect real model quality differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Noise floors may prove small (well-curated benchmarks), validating small-delta claims and confining the critique to noisier datasets.
fastest_falsification: Re-score existing public model outputs against any existing alternative annotation versions of a benchmark subset: days if such versions exist.

one_line: Mean-mIoU winners regress on a third of images: per-image regression rate disagrees with aggregate rankings and matters more for deployment.
problem: Model selection uses dataset-mean metrics; deployments experience per-image quality, and a mean-better model that regresses on many images may be operationally worse, a phenomenon nobody quantifies.
core_hypothesis: For typical method-pair comparisons with modest mean deltas, the per-image regression fraction is large (often near half), regression images are structured rather than random, and ranking by regression-rate frequently disagrees with ranking by mean.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 10 published-style model pairs, at least 30% of images will regress for the mean-winner in the median pair, and regression-rate ordering will disagree with mean ordering in at least 3 of 10 pairs.
why_important: Introduces regression accounting (standard in software engineering) into segmentation evaluation; constructive deliverable is a co-primary reliability metric that deployment teams can adopt immediately.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: per-image win-loss analysis appears rare in segmentation papers; regression-rate as a co-primary metric proposal appears new (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-image deltas for public checkpoint pairs on standard benchmarks; report regression fractions, cluster regressed images, compare orderings under both metrics.
main_risk: Per-image IoU is noisy for small-object images; needs image-level significance filtering to avoid counting metric noise as regression.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: A model with higher dataset-mean mIoU is the better model for use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regression fractions may be small and unstructured for most pairs, confirming mean metrics as sufficient in practice.
fastest_falsification: Per-image differencing of existing public predictions: one day.

one_line: Region-metric and boundary-metric rankings diverge enough to flip method orderings, so mIoU-only leaderboards are selecting against boundary quality.
problem: The community optimizes and ranks by mIoU while asserting that better mIoU implies generally better masks; if boundary-metric orderings diverge systematically, downstream users optimizing for edit quality or safety margins are misled.
core_hypothesis: Method families differ in how they buy mIoU (region filling versus boundary precision); re-scoring leaderboard checkpoints with boundary-F will reveal frequent ranking inversions, and the divergence grows with architectural distance between methods.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-scoring 15 public checkpoints on two benchmarks will show boundary-F rank correlation with mIoU below 0.7 and at least 4 top-ten inversions, with query-based and per-pixel families systematically trading places.
why_important: If rankings are metric-relative in a structured way, benchmark culture needs dual-metric reporting; users get a decision rule (choose family by target metric) rather than a single false ordering.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: boundary metrics exist and are occasionally reported; the systematic ranking-divergence claim across model families appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Batch re-scoring of a public checkpoint zoo with region and boundary metrics; correlation and inversion analysis by architecture family.
main_risk: Boundary-metric implementations vary; the study must fix and release one canonical implementation to be citable.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: mIoU ordering is a sufficient proxy for overall mask quality ordering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Metrics may correlate above 0.9 across modern models, making mIoU-only culture harmless in practice.
fastest_falsification: Re-scoring existing predictions with a boundary metric: one to two days.

one_line: Small-object segmentation leaderboards measure annotation noise: below an area threshold, GT boundary placement error exceeds model differences.
problem: Papers claim small-object improvements using IoU on tiny instances, where a one-pixel GT boundary shift changes IoU by large fractions; the annotation-noise contribution to small-object metrics is unquantified.
core_hypothesis: For instances below a benchmark-specific pixel-area threshold, inter-annotation IoU variance exceeds typical between-model differences, meaning small-object leaderboard positions are substantially noise; above the threshold the metric becomes informative again.
falsifiable_prediction: Dual re-annotation of small instances will show inter-annotator IoU spread exceeding the median between-model IoU gap for instances under a determinable area threshold, on two benchmarks.
why_important: Constructive deliverable: area-thresholded reporting standards and noise-aware small-object metrics (distance-based rather than overlap-based), preventing a literature of noise-chasing on tiny objects.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: small-object IoU instability is folklore; the threshold quantification against model-difference distributions appears unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate stratified small-instance samples with multiple annotators; compare inter-annotator IoU spread with between-model gaps as a function of instance area; locate the informativeness threshold.
main_risk: Thresholds will vary across datasets and classes; the deliverable must be a method for computing thresholds, not one universal number.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: IoU-based small-object metrics meaningfully rank models on small-object performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern annotation tooling may place tiny boundaries reproducibly enough that the noise floor stays below model differences, validating current metrics.
fastest_falsification: Multi-annotator re-annotation of 200 small instances plus existing model outputs: annotation-bounded, about a week.

one_line: Panoptic quality differences among modern methods are recognition differences in disguise: the segmentation term is saturated and the metric misdirects research.
problem: PQ multiplies recognition and segmentation terms; if modern methods differ almost entirely on the recognition term, PQ-driven research is optimizing classification while presenting itself as mask-quality progress.
core_hypothesis: Decomposing PQ across recent method generations will show the segmentation-quality term nearly constant while recognition-quality drives the deltas; method innovations marketed as mask improvements act through detection/classification pathways.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 10 public panoptic models spanning several years, over 80% of PQ variance will be explained by the recognition term, with segmentation-term spread under 2 points.
why_important: Metric design steers fields; if PQ progress is recognition progress, mask-quality research needs its own protected metric, and past attribution of gains should be revised. Constructive: decomposed reporting as standard.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: PQ decomposition is defined in the metric itself; the variance-attribution analysis across method history appears not to have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate a chronological panoptic model zoo with decomposed PQ terms; variance analysis; check whether claimed mask-side innovations moved the segmentation term.
main_risk: Public checkpoints may not span enough method history; partial reimplementation could be needed for older methods.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: PQ improvements reflect balanced progress in both recognizing and segmenting scene elements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some method generations may show genuine segmentation-term jumps (mask-quality innovations), refuting the saturation claim for those transitions.
fastest_falsification: Decomposed re-scoring of existing panoptic predictions: one day.

one_line: Zero-shot segmentation evaluations of web-pretrained models are contaminated: benchmark imagery overlaps pretraining crawls, and post-crawl imagery exposes the inflation.
problem: Foundation models pretrained on web crawls are evaluated zero-shot on benchmarks whose images circulated on the web for years; the zero-shot label is unverified and the contamination magnitude for dense tasks is unknown.
core_hypothesis: A measurable share of zero-shot segmentation performance on standard benchmarks reflects exposure to the test images or their near-duplicates during pretraining; evaluation on verifiably post-crawl imagery of matched content will show a systematic drop.
falsifiable_prediction: Zero-shot mask quality on newly captured, content-matched imagery (scenes and classes mirroring the benchmark, photographed after the model's data cutoff) will fall below benchmark performance by a margin exceeding domain-shift controls estimated from supervised models.
why_important: Zero-shot claims anchor the foundation-model narrative; a quantified contamination correction changes model comparisons and motivates a rolling post-crawl evaluation set as community infrastructure.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: contamination studies exist for language and image classification; a dense-prediction contamination quantification with matched-content fresh captures appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture a content-matched fresh test set; evaluate zero-shot foundation segmenters and supervised control models on both; attribute the differential drop beyond the supervised-control drop to contamination.
main_risk: Matching content distribution without matching capture style is hard; the supervised-model control arm is essential and its adequacy will be debated.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Zero-shot benchmark numbers for web-pretrained models measure genuine generalization to unseen data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The differential drop may be negligible, indicating memorization contributes little to dense zero-shot performance even when exposure occurred.
fastest_falsification: Near-duplicate search of one benchmark test set against public crawl indexes to bound exposure rates: days, before any capture effort.

one_line: Cross-dataset generalization tables measure taxonomy-mapping choices as much as model robustness: remapping ambiguity moves results more than method differences.
problem: Cross-dataset evaluation requires mapping label taxonomies (which classes count as equivalent); papers make undocumented mapping choices, and the sensitivity of generalization conclusions to those choices is unknown.
core_hypothesis: For common cross-dataset pairs, varying the label mapping within defensible alternatives changes measured generalization by more than typical between-method differences, meaning parts of the generalization literature rank mapping conventions rather than models.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 5 defensible mapping variants for two standard cross-dataset pairs, the within-model score spread will exceed the between-model spread of published-style comparisons on the same pairs.
why_important: Constructive deliverable: a published canonical mapping suite with sensitivity ranges, making cross-dataset claims reproducible; without it, generalization comparisons are not interpretable.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: mapping issues are acknowledged in passing; a formal sensitivity analysis quantifying their share of measured generalization appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define mapping variants from dataset documentation ambiguities; re-score a model zoo across variants; compare mapping-induced spread with model-induced spread.
main_risk: Defensibility of mapping variants is subjective; variants must be derived from documented dataset definitions by independent judges.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Cross-dataset mIoU comparisons measure model generalization robustly enough to rank methods.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mapping-induced spread may be small for the well-trodden dataset pairs, confining the problem to exotic evaluations.
fastest_falsification: Two mapping variants on one dataset pair with existing predictions: one day.

one_line: Humans disagree with mIoU about which segmentation is better: at matched scores, perceptual preference is driven by error structure the metric ignores.
problem: mIoU treats all misclassified pixels equally; humans judging mask quality weight boundary jaggedness, scattered false blobs, and semantic implausibility differently, and the correlation between metric and preference has not been established for modern models.
core_hypothesis: For model pairs within 1 mIoU of each other, human preference will systematically favor outputs with coherent errors (fewer scattered components, plausible shapes) over higher-mIoU outputs with structurally ugly errors, revealing a metric-preference divergence exploitable for metric design.
falsifiable_prediction: In forced-choice studies over matched-mIoU output pairs, human preference will deviate from mIoU ordering in over 35% of comparisons, and a structure-aware metric (component count, boundary smoothness, shape plausibility) will predict preference significantly better than mIoU.
why_important: Perceptual metrics reshaped image synthesis research; segmentation evaluation may need the same correction, especially for human-facing applications (editing, medical review). Constructive: a preference-calibrated composite metric.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: human studies of segmentation quality exist in specialized domains; a general metric-vs-preference divergence quantification for modern models appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect forced-choice judgments (crowd plus expert) on matched-mIoU output pairs from public models; fit preference predictors; compare mIoU against structure-aware alternatives.
main_risk: Preference depends on task framing (editing vs safety review); the study needs at least two framings to claim generality.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Higher mIoU means better segmentation as humans would judge it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Preference may track mIoU closely once deltas exceed noise, making the divergence a curiosity confined to ties.
fastest_falsification: Pilot forced-choice study on 100 matched pairs from existing predictions: under a week including collection.

one_line: Open-vocabulary segmentation is high-resource-vocabulary segmentation: per-class performance tracks caption-word frequency more than visual difficulty.
problem: Open-vocabulary models are presented as handling arbitrary class names; if performance is governed by how often a class name appears in web captions, the openness claim is a frequency illusion with predictable failure on rare vocabulary.
core_hypothesis: Per-class zero-shot segmentation quality is better predicted by the class name's estimated caption-corpus frequency than by visual-difficulty covariates (size, texture distinctiveness, boundary complexity); low-frequency names fail regardless of visual ease.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-class zero-shot IoU on name-frequency estimates and visual covariates across 200+ classes will assign dominant explanatory weight to frequency, and visually-easy but rarely-named classes will underperform visually-hard but common classes.
why_important: Defines what open-vocabulary actually delivers and yields a constructive artifact: a frequency-controlled benchmark that measures true generalization to rare vocabulary rather than lexical familiarity.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: frequency effects are documented for VLM classification in places; a frequency-vs-visual-difficulty decomposition for dense open-vocabulary prediction appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble per-class results for 2 public open-vocab segmenters; estimate name frequencies from a public caption corpus; fit and compare regression models with visual covariates.
main_risk: Frequency estimates from proxy corpora may mismatch actual training data of the models; needs at least two frequency sources for robustness.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Open-vocabulary segmenters generalize to arbitrary class names via vision-language alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compositional language understanding may let models handle rare names built from common parts, weakening the raw-frequency effect.
fastest_falsification: Regression analysis on existing per-class published or reproduced results: two days.

one_line: Language embeddings add nothing for closed-set segmentation: swapping CLIP text classifiers for learned vectors changes nothing but the story.
problem: Closed-set segmentation models increasingly use text-embedding classifiers for a language-aligned framing; whether language structure contributes anything when the label set is fixed is untested.
core_hypothesis: For fixed label sets, text-derived classifier weights are just an initialization of class vectors; replacing them with freely learned vectors (or random-init vectors trained identically) will match performance, showing the language alignment is decorative in the closed-set regime.
falsifiable_prediction: Learned-vector variants will match text-embedding variants within 0.2 mIoU on two closed-set benchmarks across two architectures, including on class subsets with semantically related names where language structure should help most.
why_important: Deflates a marketing-level belief and sharpens the real question (when does language help dense prediction), preventing misattribution of gains to language alignment in closed-set papers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: this control experiment is cheap and obvious yet appears unreported in the closed-set-with-text-heads literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train text-head and learned-head twins on two benchmarks; compare aggregate and semantically-clustered class subsets; 3 seeds.
main_risk: Very-low-data classes might genuinely benefit from text priors; the claim should be scoped to standard data regimes with a low-data arm reported separately.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Language-aligned classifier heads bring semantic structure that improves closed-set segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Text embeddings may act as a useful regularizer for rare classes even closed-set, producing a real gap in the tail.
