fastest_falsification: One twin pair on one benchmark: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Scaling the language side of vision-language models does not improve segmentation grounding: localization is bottlenecked by the vision encoder.
problem: The community scales LLM components of multimodal models expecting broad capability gains; for pixel-grounding tasks the binding constraint may be entirely in visual representation resolution and quality.
core_hypothesis: Across VLM families, swapping in larger language models at fixed vision encoders leaves segmentation/grounding metrics flat, while modest vision-side resolution or encoder improvements move them substantially; language scale only improves the linguistic wrapper (descriptions, formats).
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial over language-model size and vision-encoder setting will show grounding-mask quality variance dominated by the vision factor, with language-size main effect under seed noise except on linguistically complex referring expressions.
why_important: Anti-scaling guidance for multimodal budget allocation: pixel-level capabilities need vision investment, not LLM scale; corrects extrapolation from language-benchmark scaling to dense grounding.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: component-wise scaling attribution for dense grounding appears unpublished; most scaling reports aggregate over task types.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use an open VLM family with interchangeable components; run the 2-factor grid on referring segmentation and grounding benchmarks; variance decomposition.
main_risk: Component interfaces confound the factorial (retraining adapters per cell); adapters must be retrained identically per cell to keep the comparison fair.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Bigger language models make multimodal systems better across tasks, including pixel grounding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Complex referring expressions may be common enough in practice that language-side gains matter operationally, even if simple grounding is vision-bound.
fastest_falsification: Two language sizes at one vision setting on one grounding benchmark: a few GPU-days with open components.

one_line: Referring-expression segmentation models ignore relational language: swapping spatial relations changes few predictions.
problem: Referring segmentation is assumed to require compositional language understanding; models may instead resolve referents through category and salience priors, treating the relational content as noise.
core_hypothesis: For expressions containing spatial relations, systematically inverting the relation (left/right, above/below, in front of/behind) will leave the majority of predicted masks unchanged, revealing that relational words are largely unread; accuracy on relation-critical cases (multiple same-category instances) will approach coin-flip.
falsifiable_prediction: On relation-inverted probe sets, fewer than 40% of predictions will change appropriately, and multi-instance relation-critical accuracy will be within 10 points of chance for at least two public models.
why_important: Exposes a capability gap masked by benchmark composition (most expressions are resolvable without relations) and provides a constructive probe suite for training relation-sensitive grounding.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: relation-insensitivity findings exist for VQA and retrieval; a controlled inversion protocol for segmentation-grade grounding appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build relation-inverted paired probes from existing referring datasets (filter to multi-instance images); evaluate public models on prediction-change and correctness metrics.
main_risk: Automatically inverting relations can create infelicitous expressions; human validation of probe naturalness is required.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Referring segmentation models parse and use the compositional structure of expressions, including spatial relations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Recent instruction-tuned grounding models may handle relations well, in which case the probe certifies progress instead of exposing failure.
fastest_falsification: 500 inverted probes on one public model: two days including probe construction.

one_line: Caption supervision teaches nameability, not segmentability: language-supervised features underperform on visually-coherent but rarely-named regions.
problem: Language-supervised pretraining is assumed to produce generally better semantic features; captions systematically under-describe certain visual phenomena (shadows, stains, reflections, material transitions), which may create structured feature blind spots.
core_hypothesis: Regions that humans segment consistently but rarely name (shadow boundaries, wetness, wear patterns) will be represented worse by caption-supervised features than by self-supervised features at matched scale, because caption gradients never reward distinguishing them.
falsifiable_prediction: Frozen-feature probes on a rarely-named-region benchmark (shadow, stain, reflection masks) will favor SSL features over caption-supervised features by a clear margin, reversing their ordering on standard named-category benchmarks.
why_important: Identifies a systematic defect of the dominant pretraining paradigm with consequences for any downstream task needing non-nameable structure (robotics traversability, inspection), and motivates hybrid objectives constructively.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: lexical bias of caption supervision is discussed conceptually; a probe-based blind-spot quantification on non-nameable dense structure appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble or reuse shadow/stain/reflection mask data; run frozen probes for matched caption-supervised and SSL checkpoints; compare orderings against named-category controls.
main_risk: Matched-scale checkpoint pairs across supervision types are imperfect; the comparison needs at least two model pairs to be persuasive.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Caption-supervised features are semantically superior all-around for dense understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Web captions may mention these phenomena more than assumed (photography commentary), giving caption models adequate signal and nullifying the blind spot.
fastest_falsification: Frozen probes on existing shadow-detection datasets with two public checkpoint pairs: days.

one_line: Prompt-template engineering for open-vocabulary segmentation is dataset-specific noise: template gains do not transfer across benchmarks.
problem: Papers report meaningful gains from prompt templates (context words, ensembling) for open-vocab dense prediction, and these templates are copied as best practice; whether template gains generalize across datasets is untested.
core_hypothesis: Template-induced gains are overfitted to per-benchmark class-name statistics and image styles; the cross-dataset rank correlation of template effectiveness is near zero, so template engineering is per-benchmark tuning masquerading as method.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating 20 templates across 4 benchmarks will show near-zero rank correlation of template orderings between benchmark pairs, with the best template per benchmark beating the worst by points but no template consistently in the top quartile.
why_important: Kills a pseudo-method category if confirmed (report template-marginalized results instead), or identifies genuinely robust templates if refuted; either way it cleans up evaluation practice.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: template sensitivity is known; the cross-dataset transferability of template rankings for dense tasks appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid of templates x benchmarks x 2 models, inference only; rank-correlation analysis and template-marginalized reporting proposal.
main_risk: Template effects may interact with model choice more than benchmark choice, requiring the model dimension in the grid.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Good prompt templates are a transferable ingredient that reliably improves open-vocabulary dense prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A few templates may be robustly good (generic context words), showing partial transferability and salvaging the practice.
fastest_falsification: Inference-only template grid: two or three days.

one_line: Visual in-context segmentation generalizes by low-level appearance matching, not concept transfer: recoloring the example breaks it.
problem: Visual in-context learners (segment new images given one example image-mask pair) are described with language borrowed from LLM in-context learning, implying abstract task inference; the mechanism may be nearest-neighbor appearance propagation.
core_hypothesis: In-context mask quality will collapse under example-target appearance divergence (recoloring, texture swap, style transfer of the example) while remaining stable under semantic-preserving appearance-matched changes, demonstrating appearance matching rather than concept-level task inference.
falsifiable_prediction: Recolored or restyled example pairs (same concept, shifted appearance) will reduce in-context segmentation IoU by over 40% relative, while equally large semantic changes with matched appearance statistics reduce it far less.
why_important: Corrects an anthropomorphic capability narrative and defines the actual generalization envelope of visual in-context systems, guiding when practitioners can trust one-shot mask specification.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: appearance-vs-concept probing of visual in-context segmentation appears unpublished; the ICL framing has spread faster than mechanism analysis.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct controlled example-perturbation suites (color, texture, style, semantic swaps) and evaluate public in-context segmenters across perturbation types.
main_risk: Perturbation methods introduce artifacts; needs perceptual-quality controls so degradation is attributable to appearance shift, not artifact confusion.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Visual in-context learning infers the task concept from the example and applies it abstractly to new images.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models trained with heavy augmentation may be genuinely appearance-invariant, passing the recoloring probe and supporting the concept-transfer reading.
fastest_falsification: Recoloring probe on one public in-context model: two days.

one_line: Negation in language-guided segmentation does not improve with scale: absence semantics is structurally missing from caption supervision at every size.
problem: Language-guided segmenters fail on negated queries (the chair without cushions, cars that are not red); scaling is the community's default answer to capability gaps, but captions almost never encode absence, so scale may not touch this failure.
core_hypothesis: Negation handling is flat across model scale because the training signal for absence is absent at all corpus sizes; the failure is a data-distribution property, not a capacity property, and only targeted supervision (contrastive negation pairs) moves it.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a scale ladder of language-guided segmenters, negated-query accuracy will remain within a few points of the smallest model (and near the ignore-the-negation baseline), while a small targeted negation fine-tune moves it more than the entire scale ladder.
why_important: Anti-scaling evidence with a constructive remedy: identifies a capability wall that compute cannot climb and demonstrates the data-centric fix, informing both research strategy and product claims about language-driven segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: negation blindness is documented for CLIP-style retrieval; the scale-invariance claim plus targeted-fix comparison for dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a negation probe set from existing datasets (attribute-negated and object-negated queries); evaluate a scale ladder; fine-tune the mid-size model on synthetic negation pairs; compare deltas.
main_risk: Constructing unambiguous negated queries with clean mask ground truth requires care; ambiguous probes would blur the scale-flatness measurement.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Language-understanding weaknesses in multimodal systems, including negation, improve with model and data scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Emergent compositional handling at the largest scales could produce a late jump the mid-scale ladder misses.
fastest_falsification: Negation probe evaluation on two model sizes: days after probe construction.

one_line: Zero-shot-on-novel-classes claims are synonym leakage: truly novel coined categories drop open-vocab models to near chance.
problem: Open-vocabulary evaluations declare classes novel if excluded from fine-tuning vocabulary, ignoring that the classes appear under synonyms and hypernyms throughout web-scale pretraining; genuine novelty is never tested.
core_hypothesis: Performance on declared-novel classes is carried by lexical-semantic overlap with pretraining vocabulary; on genuinely novel categories (coined names for visually definable but unnamed concepts, defined by example or description), open-vocab segmenters approach chance while humans perform well from the same definitions.
falsifiable_prediction: On a coined-category benchmark (new names with visual definitions like specific part-configurations or damage types), open-vocab models given the definitions will score under 25% of their declared-novel-class performance, while human annotators exceed 80% agreement from the same definitions.
why_important: Redefines what zero-shot means for dense prediction and supplies a benchmark protocol (coined categories with definitional grounding) that measures the capability the field claims to have.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: synonym-leakage critiques exist for zero-shot classification; a coined-category dense benchmark with human baselines appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 20 coined categories with textual and exemplar definitions; annotate 500 images; evaluate open-vocab segmenters (text-only and text-plus-exemplar prompting) against human performance.
main_risk: Coined categories must be fair (visually learnable from definitions); pilot human studies are needed to certify learnability before judging models.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Open-vocabulary segmenters generalize to genuinely unseen categories given a name or description.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Description-based prompting may compose known attributes well enough to handle coined categories, revealing real compositional generalization.
fastest_falsification: Pilot with 5 coined categories on 100 images: one week including annotation.

one_line: LLM-agent segmentation pipelines lose to one fine-tuned model at matched compute everywhere except genuinely compositional queries, which are rare.
problem: Agentic pipelines (LLM planning over segmentation tools) are proposed as the future interface for dense tasks; their accuracy-per-FLOP against a single fine-tuned end-to-end model is unmeasured, and the query distribution where agents pay off is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: For the overwhelming majority of practical segmentation queries (single class or referring expressions), agent pipelines add latency, error-compounding tool chains, and no accuracy; their advantage exists only on multi-step compositional queries that are a small fraction of realistic workloads.
falsifiable_prediction: On a query distribution sampled from realistic annotation and editing logs, an end-to-end model will beat an agent pipeline at matched total compute on over 85% of queries, with the agent winning only on the compositional tail (multi-constraint, counting-dependent, or iterative queries).
why_important: Provides the missing cost-benefit boundary for a heavily hyped architecture class; the constructive output is a query-complexity router that invokes agents only where they pay. Flag: LLM/agent territory is scheduled for wave 3; this single idea is included as a contrarian claim and should be deduplicated against wave-3 shards.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: agent-vs-end-to-end compute-matched comparisons with realistic query distributions appear unpublished for segmentation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a realistic query set; run one open agent pipeline and one fine-tuned grounding segmenter at matched compute; stratify outcomes by query complexity class.
main_risk: Realistic query distributions are hard to source; using synthetic distributions would beg the question, so logs or user studies are needed.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Agentic LLM-orchestrated pipelines are the coming superior interface for language-driven segmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agent pipelines improve rapidly with tool and prompt quality; the crossover could move toward agents faster than a static study captures.
fastest_falsification: 100-query pilot across both pipelines with complexity labels: under a week.

one_line: INT8 quantization is not free for segmentation: negligible mIoU cost hides multi-fold boundary-band damage.
problem: Quantization reports for segmentation cite sub-point mIoU drops and declare success; mIoU is area-dominated and structurally insensitive to boundary-band errors where quantization noise plausibly concentrates.
core_hypothesis: Post-training quantization error concentrates at decision boundaries in feature space, which map to spatial boundary bands; boundary-F degradation will be several times larger (relatively) than mIoU degradation, harming exactly the applications (editing, medical margins) that quantize for deployment.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 4 models and 2 benchmarks, INT8 post-training quantization will show relative boundary-F degradation at least 3x the relative mIoU degradation, with the gap widening at INT4.
why_important: Deployment sign-offs rely on the quantization-is-free belief; a spatially structured damage profile changes acceptance testing and motivates boundary-aware calibration (the constructive companion experiment).
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: quantization studies report aggregate metrics; boundary-stratified damage profiles for dense models appear unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantize public checkpoints with standard toolchains; evaluate region and boundary metrics plus distance-to-boundary-stratified error; test boundary-aware calibration as remedy.
main_risk: Damage profiles may be architecture-dependent (CNN vs ViT), requiring both families before generalizing.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: INT8 quantization costs segmentation models almost nothing in output quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Quantization noise may act as uniform smoothing with no boundary concentration, keeping the damage proportional and the belief intact.
fastest_falsification: Quantize two public checkpoints and run stratified evaluation: two days.

one_line: Pruning results from classification do not transfer: at matched sparsity, segmentation loses disproportionately and structured pruning removes boundary-critical filters first.
problem: Pruning ratios and lottery-ticket-style claims validated on classification are applied to dense models with the same expectations; dense prediction may depend on exactly the high-frequency, low-magnitude filters that magnitude pruning removes.
core_hypothesis: Prunability is task-structured: at equal sparsity, segmentation degrades several times more than classification on the same backbone, and pruned-filter analysis will show boundary-frequency filters over-represented among casualties.
falsifiable_prediction: At 80% sparsity, a shared backbone will retain most of its classification accuracy but lose disproportionate segmentation quality, with boundary-F losses exceeding mIoU losses, and frequency analysis of removed filters will confirm high-frequency bias.
why_important: Corrects the assumption that compression recipes are task-portable, and yields a constructive dense-specific pruning criterion (protect high-frequency filters) with immediate deployment value.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: task-dependent prunability is partially explored; a boundary-frequency mechanism account for dense-task pruning fragility appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Prune one backbone at several sparsities; fine-tune matched heads for classification and segmentation; compare degradation curves; analyze removed-filter frequency content.
main_risk: Fine-tuning after pruning partially heals damage differently per task, complicating attribution; needs both with and without healing arms.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Pruning ratios that preserve classification accuracy preserve downstream dense-task quality too.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Over-parameterization may be so large that dense tasks also tolerate high sparsity, with earlier reports of fragility reflecting recipe issues.
fastest_falsification: One sparsity level, both tasks, one backbone: a few GPU-days.

one_line: Distillation transfers the teacher's failure map more than its skill: distilled students are accuracy-similar but error-correlated, destroying ensemble and audit value.
problem: Knowledge distillation is evaluated by student accuracy; the structure of student errors relative to teacher errors is ignored, though it determines ensemble diversity, failure independence, and the safety value of model redundancy.
core_hypothesis: Distilled segmentation students replicate teacher error maps at high spatial correlation even when ground-truth labels are present in training; accuracy-matched students trained without distillation are far less error-correlated with the teacher, so distillation silently buys accuracy with correlation.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-pixel error-overlap between teacher and distilled student will exceed that between teacher and independently trained accuracy-matched student by at least 2x, and teacher-student ensembles will gain far less than teacher-independent ensembles at matched member accuracy.
why_important: Redundant perception stacks and cross-checking pipelines assume failure independence; distillation-induced correlation undermines them invisibly, which matters for safety architectures built on model disagreement.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: error-correlation costs of distillation appear unquantified for dense prediction; evaluation culture only tracks marginal accuracy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train distilled and independent students to matched accuracy; compute spatial error-overlap statistics and ensemble gains; repeat across two teacher architectures.
main_risk: Matching student accuracy across arms precisely is fiddly; small accuracy mismatches must be shown not to drive the correlation differences.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Distillation is a free compression tool whose only relevant output is student accuracy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ground-truth supervision during distillation may dominate gradients enough that students diverge from teacher errors, keeping correlation near the independent baseline.
fastest_falsification: Error-overlap analysis on existing public teacher-student pairs: two days without training.

one_line: Token pruning and merging for ViT segmenters silently deletes small and rare objects while aggregate metrics stay green.
problem: Token-reduction papers report near-unchanged mIoU at large FLOP savings; small-object and rare-class performance, where a few tokens carry all the evidence, is not stratified in these reports.
core_hypothesis: Importance-based token reduction systematically drops tokens covering small instances and rare textures (low attention mass, unfamiliar statistics); class- and size-stratified evaluation will reveal catastrophic drops hidden by area-weighted aggregates.
falsifiable_prediction: At published-style token-reduction ratios, small-instance recall will drop by over 20% relative and bottom-decile class IoU by over 15% relative, while overall mIoU stays within 1 point, across two token-reduction methods.
why_important: Token reduction is being deployed for cost; if it deletes exactly the safety-critical content (small distant objects), acceptance criteria must add stratified gates; constructive deliverable is a worst-class-retention metric for efficiency papers.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: token-reduction evaluations appear aggregate-only for dense tasks; stratified damage profiles seem unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply two public token-reduction methods to a ViT segmenter; evaluate with instance-size and class-frequency stratification; correlate dropped-token locations with failure locations.
main_risk: Dense-task token reduction implementations vary in where reduction is applied (encoder depth), so results need a depth-position sweep.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Token reduction preserves dense-prediction quality at large compute savings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reduction schedules that keep high-resolution early layers may protect small objects, showing the damage is implementation-specific rather than inherent.
fastest_falsification: One method, stratified evaluation: two days.

one_line: Dynamic-compute segmentation allocates less compute exactly where difficulty lives: gate signals are area-dominated and starve boundaries.
problem: Early-exit and dynamic-depth models claim to spend compute where it is needed; for dense prediction the gating signals aggregate over regions, and large easy interiors may dominate them, inverting the intended allocation.
core_hypothesis: Per-region compute allocation in dynamic segmentation models anti-correlates with per-pixel difficulty: boundary bands and small objects receive relatively less marginal compute than easy interiors because gate statistics are area-weighted, so dynamic models lose precisely the hard-pixel accuracy they claim to protect.
falsifiable_prediction: Instrumenting two dynamic-compute segmenters will show compute-per-pixel negatively or negligibly correlated with error probability, and their accuracy deficit versus static twins will concentrate in boundary bands and small instances.
why_important: Reveals a design flaw in an entire efficiency genre and points to the fix (difficulty-weighted gating signals), with direct consequences for latency-constrained safety systems.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: spatial compute-allocation audits of dynamic dense models appear unpublished; papers report aggregate accuracy-latency points.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument public dynamic-segmentation models to log per-region compute; correlate with error maps; compare stratified accuracy against static baselines at matched average FLOPs.
main_risk: Few strong public dynamic-compute segmenters exist; may require reimplementing one representative method faithfully.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Dynamic computation spends capacity where the input is hard, preserving quality at lower average cost.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some gating designs operate at patch granularity fine enough to track boundaries, in which case allocation correlates positively with difficulty and the genre is vindicated.
fastest_falsification: Instrument one public dynamic model and correlate compute with errors: days.

one_line: Efficient-attention approximations validated on classification break dense prediction: approximation error lands on the high-frequency attention structure boundaries need.
problem: Linear and low-rank attention variants are marketed as task-general after classification-level validation; dense prediction may depend on precisely the sharp, local, high-rank attention patterns the approximations discard.
core_hypothesis: Attention maps relevant to boundary delineation are high-frequency and locally precise; efficient approximations preserve global averaged patterns (enough for classification) but destroy the boundary-relevant structure, producing a task-conditional failure the validation practice never sees.
falsifiable_prediction: Swapping efficient attention into a segmentation backbone at matched pretraining will cost several times more boundary-F (relatively) than classification accuracy on the same backbone, and attention-map spectral analysis will show the approximation error concentrated in high-frequency components.
why_important: Prevents silent quality loss as efficient attention spreads through deployment stacks, and gives efficiency researchers a dense-task acceptance test; the spectral mechanism is reusable scientific content.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: dense-task costs of efficient attention are anecdotally suspected; a controlled matched-pretraining comparison with mechanism analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched full/efficient attention twins; evaluate classification and segmentation heads; spectral-decompose attention approximation errors and correlate with spatial error maps.
main_risk: Efficient-attention variants differ widely; at least three representative families are needed to support a genre-level claim.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Efficient attention mechanisms preserve model quality across task types at large compute savings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hybrid designs (local windows plus linear global) may retain boundary-relevant structure fully, confining the failure to pure-approximation variants.
fastest_falsification: One efficient variant vs full attention on one segmentation benchmark with matched small-scale pretraining: about a GPU-week.

one_line: Input-resolution reduction degrades segmentation non-linearly with a predictable knee set by the instance-size distribution, breaking the graceful-degradation deployment assumption.
problem: Edge deployments reduce input resolution assuming smooth quality-cost tradeoffs; if degradation has a knee (collapse once typical instances fall below a pixel threshold), naive resolution planning fails badly on some domains.
core_hypothesis: Per-class quality versus resolution follows a sigmoid with a knee at a characteristic pixels-per-instance value; the dataset-level curve is a mixture of class sigmoids, so the safe-resolution point is predictable from instance-size statistics without exhaustive evaluation, and cross-domain transfer of resolution settings is unsafe.
falsifiable_prediction: Knee locations extracted from resolution sweeps will be predicted (rank correlation above 0.8) by median instance pixel-size per class, and datasets with small-instance-heavy distributions will show collapse at resolutions where large-instance datasets lose almost nothing.
why_important: Turns resolution planning from trial-and-error into a computable rule (constructive scaling law), and warns against the common practice of copying resolution settings across deployment domains.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: resolution ablations exist per paper; a knee-prediction law from instance statistics across datasets appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resolution sweeps for 3 models across 4 datasets with diverse instance-size distributions; fit per-class sigmoids; test knee predictability from GT size statistics.
main_risk: Knee sharpness may vary with architecture (patch size effects), requiring the law to carry an architecture term.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Segmentation quality degrades smoothly and forgivingly as input resolution is reduced.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern multi-scale training may flatten the knees into genuinely smooth curves, validating the graceful-degradation assumption.
fastest_falsification: Resolution sweep on two datasets with contrasting instance-size profiles: days, inference only.

one_line: Compressed models lose out-of-distribution robustness first: quantization and pruning trade away exactly the redundancy that provided shift tolerance.
problem: Compression is validated in-distribution; the lossless-compression narrative may hold on the test set while the compressed model's robustness margin under distribution shift quietly collapses, an interaction the deployment pipeline never measures.
core_hypothesis: Redundant capacity in over-parameterized segmenters acts as shift insurance; compression removes it, so quality degradation under shift (weather, sensor, geography) is much steeper for compressed models than their in-distribution parity with full models suggests.
falsifiable_prediction: Quantized and pruned models matched to full-precision twins in-distribution (within 0.3 mIoU) will degrade at least 50% more (relative) on shifted test sets, with the robustness gap growing monotonically with compression ratio.
why_important: Edge deployments face both compression pressure and the wildest input distributions; documenting the compression-robustness interaction forces shifted-set acceptance testing into compression practice and quantifies the true cost of efficiency.
why_possibly_novel: HYPOTHESIS, unverified: compression-robustness interactions have been studied for classification with mixed findings; a systematic dense-prediction study across compression types and shift types appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a compression grid (2 methods x 3 ratios) on two segmenters; evaluate in-distribution and on 3 shifted sets; plot robustness retention versus compression ratio.
main_risk: Robust conclusions need compression-ratio matching across methods (equal FLOPs or equal params), which existing toolchains make awkward.
territory: Negative results + contrarian (community beliefs that may be false; non-replication hypotheses; anti-scaling claims)
default_community_belief: Compression that preserves benchmark accuracy preserves model behavior generally, including under shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compression may act as regularization that helps under some shifts, producing a mixed or even reversed interaction.
fastest_falsification: One quantized/full pair evaluated on one shifted set: one day, inference only.
